utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I raise something in private session for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust the Chamber has a summary of this morning's date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Kucan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start the testimony, the witness is -- before we start the testimony, may the witness's exhibits be given a general number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, you are Milan Kucan, president of Slovenia between April/May of 1990 and the year 2002, having been elected three times to that office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Other matters of your history, of course, well-known as a matter of public record and are contained, for the assistance of the Chamber, in summary at Exhibit 447, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course this witness could deal with enormous numbers of background matters. We don't propose to do anything except take him through the critical and significant events, in light both of pressure of court and his time and also because the Chamber is already very well-informed from other evidence on many matters of background.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn first, Mr. Kucan, to the Central Committee meeting of the 30th of January of 1989, the Central Committee of the League of Communists that was held in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will find that we have for this a translation of a speech made by the accused. It's at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to look at that speech, Mr. Kucan, can you just give us the setting for what was happening there. What were the issues being focused on at that committee meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was a period when the crisis in Yugoslavia reached its culmination. It was a crisis which was multi-faceted. It was not just a political, economic crisis or a crisis between the relations of nations and ethnicities but also a crisis of social values. By then, the recognition became obvious that changes are indeed needed in Yugoslavia. The Slovenian political leadership conceived and understood these changes as a new agreement about a common life within Yugoslavia. And then within the direction of a new definition of the common interests and the common life. The then Serbian political leadership was thinking along a different line, which is that changes are indeed necessary, that changes in terms of persons and personalities should be made in the first place to thus achieve support for the changes that the Serbian political leadership had been advocating. Changes in persons and personalities, in fact, were made also through the organisation of large mass meetings and rallies through which first the leadership of Vojvodina was replaced, then the leadership of Montenegro. And at this session of the Central Committee we initially discussed the issue whether we should talk about the political circumstances and constitutional changes and amendments with the new leadership which brought about a new relation of power within the Central Committee or with the former leadership that had represented their League of Communists on the Central Committee. It is within this context that the discussion went on which the Prosecutor has referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the accused the keynote speaker at this event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No. He was one of the speakers. The keynote speaker was the then president of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, Stipe Suvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the accused made a significant speech, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which we have in B/C/S for the witness and which we can, I hope, put up in English. We can't put it up in English. We have it only in English at tab 2 of Exhibit -- I've forgotten the number already -- 447. And if Your Honours would be good enough to go with me through certain highlighted passages, Ms. Wee will, on the B/C/S version, take the witness, if he's able to see it on the screen at this stage, to the same passages and I'll ask his comments on those passages later. Within tab 2, if the Chamber would be good enough, please, to go to page 2, a third of the way down, there is a passage reading as follows: "Things that cannot be changed institutionally, and they must be changed because people don't like them or they lasted for too long, will be changed uninstitutionally. It's always been like that in any society." If the Chamber would then turn on to page 4, and the middle paragraph: "Therefore, I would like to say to all those who obviously cannot easily get rid of their habits to judge Serbia, that Serbia is equal and united and that they should not get excited about that. Once this becomes clear to them, we should all solve the difficult problems of the Yugoslav crisis together more easily and equally." Over the page, please, in the English, to page 5, the second paragraph: "I have to say that if Yugoslavia were to be conceived as a community in which Serbia is divided into three parts and on its knees, then Serbia would be against such a community, against such a Yugoslavia. Then we would be for a different Yugoslavia. In other words, for the only possible Yugoslavia, for Yugoslavia in which everyone would be equal and, therefore, Serbia as well. In that process, we would not care at all whether somebody would call it the third, fifth, or tenth Yugoslavia." And finally, if the Chamber would turn to page 7 and the paragraph starting at the foot of the page and going over, did the speech of the accused end in this way: "This session was expected to be a session of conflicts and differences, and we shouldn't be afraid of them. They're unavoidable in order to remove obstacles and to find solutions, but procedure will not bring that solution that's big and small traps, small and big artifices, intrigues and frameups. A politics chosen by people institutionally and non-institutionally, statutory, and non-statutory, on the streets and inside, populist and elitist, with or without arguments can only reach the solution. But in any case, it is clear that it is politics for socialists non-aligned and democratic Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia where people will live unitary, equally, richer, and more cultured but above all where they will live unanimously. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, with a reminder of the speech by those extracts, what was the message you perceived the accused to be giving?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The message, to put it in very simple terms, was the following: Changes such as they had been advocated by the Serbian leadership will take place whether the institutional or non-institutional approach will be used to achieve them; i.e., whether constitutional provisions will be respected or not. And this is where we differed essentially. The dilemmas were known to one and all, but as far as these dilemmas that Yugoslavia faced at that time is concerned, we applied for different answers. We opted for different answers. Where these answers brought us is apparently very well illustrated by the current status of Slovenia, which opted for the institutional, legal, and constitutional approach, and the status and situation in other parts of the former Yugoslavia that have also become independent states by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One matter of precision. We see from the text that the accused used the words "institutionally or uninstitutionally." In your answer, you have referred to "constitutionally." In the setting in which he spoke, is there an identity or proximity between something that is non-institutional and something that is non-constitutional? If not, can you explain why you used the word "constitutional."

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: In terms of its substance, this syntax "institutional" or "non-institutional" in fact implies the respect of institutional, i.e., constitutional paths and non-constitutional paths if non-institutional approaches are opted for. This was a period of mass rallies and meetings which insisted upon and achieved replacement of leaderships through the demand of the populace on the street whereby none of us believed that the people at large should be deprived of their right to voice their dissatisfaction with the circumstances. My view at that time was that of course you can go and rally on the streets to voice your dissatisfaction, but you cannot go to the streets to devise a new concept to find a way out of the situation. In other words, for legitimate political objectives to be reached, not every means can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to express a view on the accused's attitude to the use of people demonstrating on the streets?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, at that time in Slovenia, there was no one who would believe that these mass meetings and rallies that were given different names, the Meeting of the Truth about Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo, whose situation was difficult indeed and full of trials and tribulations, or they would be called the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution. So other names were given to this. So none of us believed in Slovenia that these were spontaneous meetings and rallies. One of the meetings that was to spread the truth throughout Yugoslavia was an announced meeting on the 1st of December, 1989, to be held in Ljubljana. The leadership, the then leadership of Slovenia, the then Executive Council of the Republic of Slovenia and the Ministry for the Interior banned this meeting through the use of a provision of our law since the meeting could escalate into very serious clashes and inter-ethnic conflicts on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia. So this is the continuation of that discussion and the discussions we had had on the 20th, a session of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia which the Prosecutor referred to. Before that, we had the 17th and 18th session where we also discussed changes, including constitutional changes. My view at that time was the following: We need to reach a consensus about these issues and such very significant changes cannot be made given that tense situation in Kosovo. The answer to our reservations was the following: Consensus cannot be reached. Socialism wasn't introduced through a consensus either, and that these changes will take place even if a state of emergency would have to be declared for that to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two supplementary questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two supplementary questions on the speech of the accused to which we've been referring. First, we know that the accused made a speech in June of 1989, the 28th, I think, the Battle of Kosovo speech. Did that connect back to or resonate with this earlier speech?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: In my view, this speech had been a logic continuation of the former discussions and views that changes will take place regardless the means. In fact, this speech was held to commemorate the 500th anniversary of the Kosovo Battle, which was an important battle in the history of Europe and the Serb people. At that time it was said that through these --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive my interrupting you. On this matter the Chamber has heard a lot of evidence already and is familiar with the speech, so if you could simply answer briefly whether there is a connection between the two, and effectively you've already done so. That's all I want from you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: So my answer will be very brief, but let me just finish my thought. At that time, it was said that the Serbian people are entering again battles, as it was said, not armed battles as yet; however, this is what one could not exclude. One could anticipate that there would be armed battles to follow and that changes will take place regardless the means to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the final question is: Did you at some stage - paragraph 9 of the summary - reply to the speech that the accused had made? If so, when and to what effect? In absolute summary form, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: On the basis of an agreement reached by the Slovene delegates at this session of the Central Committee, Mr. Boris Muzic took the floor the next day to respond to these assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time, then, 1989, insofar as one can crystallise states of thinking, do you take the view that there were two concepts by which Yugoslavia was being approached, one of which was that it was a vehicle for many people to live under a single roof and the other of which was different? If so, please explain, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: In fact, what you have just described is true. However, this difference in terms of Yugoslavia was born when Yugoslavia was born itself. For some politicians in Serbia, Yugoslavia was always conceived to be the state within which a single state all Serbs could live together. Others, such as the Slovenians, the Croats, the Macedonians, and I'm now speaking particularly on behalf of the Slovenes, never understood Yugoslavia in such a sense. In fact, we conceived Yugoslavia to be a state which provides for a peaceful life, development, and well-being as well as prosperity for all peoples that live within it, on an equal footing. And throughout all the crisis situations, this difference was important, even in the period of the dictatorship which was announced in 1929 in the former Kingdom of Yugoslavia when the occupation of Yugoslavia eventually took place by the Nazis. And in fact this is what was emphasised in 1945 and after the war as well as in 1974 when the last constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber has already heard much evidence about steps taken by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbia in relation to the two autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, and this as well, very briefly - perhaps even in a sentence - can you just remind us or explain to us whether taking steps in relation to those autonomous provinces had an effect on Yugoslavia as a whole structurally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it did have an influence. This constitutional structure of the Yugoslav constitution and of the Socialist Republic of Serbia was based on the basis that in the autonomous province of Vojvodina as well as Autonomous Province of Kosovo, minorities lived. The bigger minority in Vojvodina was the Hungarian one, and in the Kosovo province the big and later prevailing minority Albanian. And in that sense, both autonomous provinces functioned as a constituent element of the Yugoslav federation. With the change of the position of these two provinces in the constitutional setup of Serbia also the constitutional make-up of the federal republic changed. With the changes of the Serbian constitution in spring 1998, the constitution was changed, amended, and essentially this was an announcement of how the changes should be attained also in Yugoslavia. Because when you reduced the importance of the provinces in the constitutional setup of Yugoslavia, the -- this is what the political leadership insisted on, and this is what was done, that on matters of Yugoslav matters, the vote remains to the two provinces. So Serbia had in fact three votes on federal matters. As I said, first the changes were introduced through mass rallies. Personnel changes took place with introduction of persons who were dedicated and devoted to the goals of the Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two topics about the army, reversed in order from in the summary to take them chronologically, but to give us context, what was the Slovenian expectation, or indeed what promises had been made to generate expectations in Slovenia about its army after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, Slovenes during the course of the Second World War, after the -- through the occupation of fascist Italy and Germany, we formed our rebel army, and it never abandoned the territory of the Republic of Slovenia. This decision was based on our conviction that this partisan army cannot be separated from its nation, which would remain totally without defence. In 1990 -- in 1943, when the highest body of Yugoslavia met, the anti-fascist council Ovnoy [phoen], the Slovene delegation, and there it was promised to also our delegation and to General Jaka Avsic, that our army would become a part of the Yugoslav party -- army and that Slovene would remain also the language of command. The Slovene army was in fact disbanded. This promise was broken. The army was disbanded, it became a part of the Yugoslav army where in communication you had the equality of languages, but the command language was the Serbian language and the principle of equality of languages as a communication -- languages of communications of use was also flagrantly clear in the trial against the four in Ljubljana, trial of the four, and formally there the trial was carried on in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I turn to my second point on the army generally, just help us so that we can understand it. A Serbian foot soldier stationed in Slovenia, would he typically be in a position to understand and communicate with ordinary Slovenians in their language or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, with a bit of an effort, he could communicate, but logically it was -- it was expected that everybody speaks in the Serbian. Not only in the army but also at the federal level, at the Constitutional Court, the Serbo-Croatian, respectively Serbian language be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 15, second topic on the army of general nature. In your judgement, did the JNA in the time of Tito have, as you described it, two homes? If so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: In a certain way, yes. This army became an ideological and a political army, and in the central parts of Yugoslavia it became as the armed force of the Communist Party which was leading the resistance. A specific situation existed in Slovenia, but it's not important for this debate. But in fact, it did have two homes. The ideological home was the -- one was Yugoslavia. That was the political home of JNA, and it was always convinced that it is a factor of unity and of the very existence of Yugoslavia. This army was absolutely dedicated to President Tito, who was both the president of the state of Yugoslavia and the president of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. At his death in 1990, the -- it remained without its father, the Supreme Commander, and then the Presidency of the state which replaced Tito, it didn't recognise this Supreme Commander, and this led to the -- this meeting between the Presidency, the formal Supreme Commander, and the leadership of the army in March 1990 where the conflicts, well-known conflicts arose concerning who is in command and who is commanding the JNA, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving so far as is possible chronologically through matters that are relevant, I want to take you next to a passage from the diary of Borisav Jovic. Before we consider, if we do, extracts from that diary, is this a book you've read and are you in a position to say whether so far as factual matters related in it, they are or are not accurate? Mr. Kucan, have you -- did you hear the question or --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Have you read Borisav Jovic's book, and insofar as it contains matters of fact of which you are aware, are you able to say whether it is accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The description of events which the president of Presidency participated as well as myself are pretty precise and correct, but for other events, his description of them I cannot ascertain whether they are exactly precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have extracted from that book some passages which we would like exhibited separately, if they may be, to be commented on by this witness, the issue of the admissibility of the book as a whole falling for later determination, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's correct. We have in fact, already, I think, said we would do that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the passages about which the witness can speak, of course can be admitted once he identifies and asserts they're accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this clip of exhibits then be given a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecutor's Exhibit 448.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will see the preface to the book. I needn't take you through that. If you'd turn on, at the bottom page numbering, to what is page 44 as it reads, we see a long extract for the 21st of September, 1989. I'm not going to go into it in full because it would take too long. I'm going to ask the witness to make some comments upon it, but I'll get the flavour of the entry before asking him those questions, and I hope that the witness has the original before him. If this is acceptable to the Chamber, he has with him a volume of the book in Slovenian, as I understand it, but unless it's essential, we prefer not to relieve him of it so he can take it back with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kucan, we're looking here at an extract for the 21st of September. And if the Chamber will follow to the second paragraph, this is at a meeting that was held with Drnovsek. "He also wants to consult with me in connection with yesterday's report in Trieste's Il Piccolo that Yugoslavia is preparing for military intervention in Slovenia." If we go further down, we see that, in the middle of the page: "The Slovenes have agreed to come in the evening at 1900: Stanovik, Kucan, Potrc, and Sinogoj." If we look a little further down, we see a passage that says -- sorry, much further down. Towards the foot of the page: "Potrc briefly explains for each controversial amendment what has been changed on the basis of our objections. In essence, everything has remained the same, nothing substantive has been approved aside from a few cosmetic changes, but he stubbornly explains that absolutely everything is in keeping with the SFRY constitution. In his opinion, what we are doing is unconstitutional. He asks that we leave them alone to responsibly complete the constitutional changes, and then let the Constitutional Court react if there is reason to do so. Unfortunately, according to the Yugoslav constitution, the Constitutional Court can conclude that a republic's constitution is not in agreement with the federal constitution and call on the republic to bring it into line ..." We turn over the page to the first fresh paragraph: "Next, I took the floor. I said very clearly that in the Presidency's assessment, the adoption of the amendments in the proposed form would constitute a direct threat to the integrity of the country and the disruption of the constitutionally established order ..." And if we go on a little bit further, we'll find just a little over halfway down the page a reference to Ante: "Ante distances himself by saying he is not familiar with all the details but he feels a timeout is necessary until the issues are fully discussed. After our mostly uniform remarks, Kucan, who is visibly agitated, asks me to explain what 'other measures at the disposal of the Presidency' means. Veljko and I explain: 'What is provided for by the constitution and by the law, nothing beyond that.' 'No, no,' he insists further, 'Just tell me exactly what you mean.'" Foot of the page, the last two lines: "We have lost our thanks --" "Kucan turns to me and says, 'How do you explain that?' Of course I do. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 'We have lost our thanks to your (meaning the Serbian) two-year public offensive against our leadership, and especially because of the letter in which you invited us to come to talk to you as long as we first accept all of your assessments and positions...'" and so on. Mr. Kucan, reminding you briefly of those -- of that meeting, in a couple of sentences can you explain to the Chamber, please, what was happening here and what you were concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Distinguished Honours, this meeting was held on the 21st of September. On the 26th of September, a session was foreseen of the government -- of the Assembly of Slovenia which would adopt amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Slovenia, and with these amendments, Slovenia wished to ensure a legal path in order of asserting its interest in the Yugoslav federation; namely, if it were -- that were not possible, in order to ensure its legal and moral right to self-determination. The adoption of these constitutional amendments, the intention was to stop that in any way possible. On the eve of the 26th of September, a session of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was convened, and they asked us to suppress both that meeting and the amendments. And this meeting also concerns that. Dr. Drnovsek was the president of the Yugoslav Presidency, and representing Slovenia and our interlocutors. The entire leadership of Slovenia was there, not only the president of the federal government but also the Minister of Defence. After requesting that we do not adopt these amendments, and as the Prosecutor has quoted, it was said that all other means would be used at their disposal. Now, my question: "What does it mean all other means will be used?" It remained unanswered. But we all knew what it implied: The state of emergency and the possible use of the army in order to ensure the -- and secure order in Slovenia. So this was how we lived in Yugoslavia the last few years. It was either accusations of counter-revolutions, anti-Yugoslav activities, and then proclaim a state of emergency and then give the authorisation to the army to suspend the legal authorities and to operate in line with the interests of those who wished to have this state of emergency introduced. And this is how we understood this meeting and the discussion we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to pass over the 22nd of September entry because of time and move to the next -- at least I am at the moment -- and move to the next topic, which is this: On the -- in January of 1990, was there the 14th Congress of the League of Communists? It was on the -- the appropriate four yearly interval but it was accelerated, so to that extent an Extraordinary Congress, and at the end of it, did your delegation walk out? Just confirm that, if you will, because I'm going to play a tape first and ask for your comments later.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: This was the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Indeed they were usually typically held every four years, and in 1990, it was a Congress year. However, in the atmosphere that existed, the atmosphere of emergency that was in the air and of extraordinary situation in Yugoslavia, this Congress that was to be an ordinary Congress was requalified into an Extraordinary Congress. And at the 18th session of the League of Communists, this proposal was turned down. Then the 20th session, upon the demand of the provincial conference of Vojvodina which called for an Extraordinary Congress, which again was refuted, and then the 22nd session which was -- which approved this being an Extraordinary Congress. And in my own -- in my own contribution, I had pointed out that this was an Extraordinary Congress against the will and stand of the Slovene delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will now play an extract from the film Death of Yugoslavia made by the BBC. May it become, I think, tab 7 of Exhibit 447.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the extract.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is the extract. It includes not only the footage of the Congress itself but observations by others. Those are available for the witness to comment on. There's not a transcript available yet - I apologise for that - it will be provided in due course, but it is in English so I hope it will not inconvenience the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The instrument Milosevic chose was the Yugoslav Communist Party. He called an Extraordinary Congress. As the delegates stood for their hymn to brotherhood and unity, they all knew that this Congress had been summoned to crush the defiant Slovenes. "[No interpretation] "Kucan had only one hope. Yugoslavia's second largest republic, Croatia. "[No interpretation] "Milosevic selected as chairman one of the leaders who owed him his career. It was the first party Congress the president of Montenegro had ever attended. "[No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Well, it was thought that the Slovenes were not brave enough to take this crucial step. "[No interpretation] "This latest example of the Serb's domineering behaviour shook the delegates from other republics. "[No interpretation] "The Serb bloc showed no mercy. In the break, the Slovenes held a crisis meeting. Kucan knew if they walked out he would be blamed for the chaos that could consume Yugoslavia. He offered a deal. "[No interpretation] "The second before the final vote was announced, I was still at the speaking podium when Ribicic requested the floor. Nobody gave him the floor. He simply walked up. "[No interpretation] "Ribicic, one of the Slovene delegates, had been primed to give them their signal. "[No interpretation] "He said, unfortunately, the Slovene delegation could not accept the Krynots [phoen] in the Central Committee.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That, unfortunately, the situation is such that we have to walk out. "[Previous translation continues]... from the presiding head table, and they started leaving the plenary session from one single door."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, does the footage we've looked at, together with the observations made, reflect the tension and difficulties of that Congress?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes, they do reflect it very faithfully, especially the round of applause that we were given when we were walking out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We saw the card voting. Did you observe something about the actions of the accused at the time of card voting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should say a few sentences before I answer this question. At this Congress, what was discussed were most crucial political questions in Yugoslavia, and what we proposed is that the discussion at the Congress should concern a concept of future living together in Yugoslavia, whether there is an interest of such living together, under what circumstances, what is this interest, and also, under what conditions to remain members of the same organisation, and that in this way political life in Yugoslavia be democratised. And the contents of the amendment that we proposed for this reason was the following: To first to endorse political pluralism that has already become a reality in Yugoslavia, then the parliamentary elections had been held in Slovenia at the time of the Congress, that political processes start evolving in Yugoslavia, then also an article of the law sanctioning the so-called verbal offence was also proposed, that all political prisoners be released, that torture be also forbidden in proceedings, and so forth. And also what we demanded is that we should go through with the logic whereby in fact communists within their individual leagues be autonomous and that it was not possible to outvote the stance or positions of any one of these organisations. There was an atmosphere in which the Slovene communists and their positions at this Congress be in fact isolated and should not receive any support from delegates from other republics and provinces. And this had happened already during the debates within the commissions or committees and also at the Congress session, and thus our amendments were largely refuted and rejected. And Milosevic, who was -- and Ribicic then said that we -- the Slovene communists could no longer see a place within such an organisation and that we were going to decide on these issues at home. So this is to briefly describe the situation once it has already culminated. I would also say the following: There were voting cards, and the accused was the first or among the first to lift it, and then this was followed by the majority at the Congress who showed the corresponding colour of their cards, and that meant rejecting the Slovene amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You already volunteered the observation that the applause at the end of the Congress, as you left, was significant. And if you want to add just a word or so about that, do, before we move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps what needs to be said is that all those who applauded us when we walked out did not really thought that this was and spelled the true dissolution of Yugoslavia or the end of it. And Ivica Racan, who was heading the Croatian Communist delegation proposed that the Congress should interrupt the session so that the necessary consultations may be carried out and that the Congress may then resume its session. And while the accused said that there should be no interruption in the deliberations of the Congress, that a new quorum should be established, a new majority whereby the Congress would adopt decisions, because if Ivica Racan's proposal were to be accepted, that would mean beheading and disbanding the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. And this is what happened. The Congress indeed had been interrupted, but it had never been resumed again. And it had also announced the end of Yugoslavia as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We turn in the summary to paragraph 26, to May of 1990 and to the disarming of the Slovenian Territorial Defence. For speed, can I ask you, please, Mr. Kucan, to look at Exhibit 447, tab 3, the English version of which can, if possible, be shown on the overhead projector. To save time, we'll abbreviate our description of this document dated the 14th of May, coming from the Secretariat for National Defence, strictly confidential, headed "The safekeeping of weapons" and ordering, under number 1, that: "The military district commands, together with TO staffs, shall organise the takeover, storage, and safekeeping of the complete stock of Territorial Defence weapons and ammunition in the JNA supply dumps and depots. Within the scope of further organisational and establishment improvements, Territorial Defence commanders shall consider the possibility of abolishing certain smaller Territorial Defence units ..." Perhaps we should look at number 2 as well further down the page. "Exceptionally, where facilities are very far away and where conditions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are not conducive to it or it is impossible to find a place for Territorial Defence weapons and ammunition ... they should be stored and safeguarded in Territorial Defence depots guarded by JNA units." And we see that this comes from General Adzic, the order to be completed by the 21st of May. If we then turn to the Jovic diary extracts, Exhibit 448, and using the page numbers at the foot, page 131 for the 17th of May, is there an entry: "We take measures to ensure that weapons are taken from civilian Territorial Defence depots in Slovenia and Croatia and transferred to military depots. We will not permit Territorial Defence weapons to be misused in any conflicts or for forcible secession. "Practically speaking, we have disarmed them. Formally, this was done by the head of the General Staff, but it was actually under our order. Extreme reaction by the Slovenes and Croatians, but they have no recourse." 18th of May: "I am at my weekend house in Niksic. In the evening Milan Kucan calls me. He complains about the seizure of weapons. He says that the people are opposed to this move, that there could be casualties. He's called a session of the Slovene Presidency over the question and he asks whether we can meet to discuss the matter. "Sure, I tell him. He should contact me Monday morning so that we can set up a meeting. By the way, I tell him, I have heard about this campaign on the radio. I do not know what is going on, but I advise him not to get into conflict with the army, to surrender the weapons and on Monday we will clear up everything, if necessary. "A rough start. They immediately summon Stipe Suvar to Zagreb to report on what we have concluded in connection with the speech before the Yugoslav Assembly." I don't think I need to finish that. We go to the 21st of May, the same page, 131. "Kucan and Drnovsek came to discuss the seizure of Slovene Territorial Defence weapons based on the Presidency decision that the weapons be seized from all republican Territorial Defences and placed under JNA control. On our side, Vjelko Kadijevic and Anton Stari beside me. "Kucan spoke at length: 'We were not notified by anyone.' The weapons were first transferred and then they learned of the action. They do not know the essence, the reasons, and the goal. They regard this as disarmament. They feel that this threatens the republic's sovereignty. He asks that they be showed the order, how it reads, and who issued it. He regards the General Staff's explanation as inadequate. He thinks that there is no basis in the constitution for such a measure. They brought the weapons, they are responsible for directing the Territorial Defence, and now they are being treated this way, without being told, and the weapons are seized. He believes this is a case of political intervention and that is a threat to their sovereign rights. Perhaps the direct cause of this is the climate that has emerged in Slovenia after my inaugural speech and the criticism of that speech in Slovenia and Croatia. The political situation in Slovenia is very serious because of the weapon seizures --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm very sorry. "He is not sure how it can be remedied. "He asks that they be accurately informed about what is going on. "That the weapons be returned to them and they will look after their storage conditions; "That the commander of the Territorial Defence for Slovenia be replaced; "That we take a look at how to reduce political tensions. "Veljko explains that the measures were taken throughout the country, not only in Slovenia, because the depots were poorly secured and the inter-ethnic and general political situation is rapidly worsening; that this is exclusively the military's jurisdiction --" I go over the brackets -- "that this is not the republic's concern, and that they, the republics, want to interfere with military questions and have no right to do so. If they provide good conditions for protecting the weapons, returning them might be considered, but that presupposes at least one armed unit and not one sentry, which in the event of an attack will repulse the seizure of weapons. All of their authorities remain, including using the weapons from the military depots for training exercise. "Naturally, Kucan was not satisfied." And then on the 21st of May: "Veljko informs me of a conversation with Ante Markovic. Spoke with him for three hours. Seems to have persuaded him to accept our plan for trying to impose legal and constitutional order. He has serious doubts about Ante Markovic's real intentions but will monitor that closely." And so on, and I think, for reasons of time, I'm going cut to my questions to you with those materials in mind. Were you aware in advance of this disarmament of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No. Nobody notified us about these plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The order that we looked at first, did you discover whether it was an order that applied to the federal Yugoslavia as a whole or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, this order, such as it is, is something that I have in front of my eyes for the first time. I had an opportunity to see an order which was issued on the basis of this order by the commander of the 5th Military District in Zagreb, and that order also had to do with the withdrawal of the arms of the Territorial Defence in Slovenia. This order was issued on the 15th of May, which is the very day on which the term of office expired of the president of the Presidency of the SFRY, Dr. Drnovsek, who represented Slovenia, and when Dr. Jovic took office as president of the Presidency on behalf of Serbia. This happened after a situation in which, through the first democratic elections held in April, we had already had elected a new Assembly, new parliament in Slovenia, and the Zagreb order entered into force on the day when our parliament sat for the first time, when our new government was elected, and when the new Presidency took oath. And I was elected during the general elections the president of the Presidency. So as far as this order is concerned, when people called in from the municipalities, telling us about this order, telling us that the army came in with the demand that they hand over the weapons, so we were -- we received this information from the people in the municipalities, and we considered this order to be an order to disarm the Slovene Territorial Defence. At a later stage, in the course of our conversations and discussions, it turned out that the argument they used was to prevent the new authorities in Slovenia to use these weapons. Let me draw your attention to the fact that this is May 1990. In formal terms, Slovenia decided and discussed its independence, its autonomy, its dissociation from Yugoslavia only when we launched preparations for the referendum of independence which was held in December 1990. So reasons to think and to believe that Slovenia could use these weapons to dissolve, by use of force, Yugoslavia were not there. And in fact, there was no theft of the weapons no Slovenia because the Slovene Territorial Defence very carefully guarded and protected its own weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Everything else that I want you to help us with in relation to the disarming has been covered by the documents we've looked at, I think, save for this: Did you have -- paragraph 27 of the summary. Did you contact General Hocevar and did he explain to you what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, this did take place. I tried to establish contact with General Hocevar. However, Your Honours, may I be allowed to say a few statements before. The Territorial Defence of Yugoslavia was part and parcel of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. It was established in 1968 after the attack of the Warsaw Pact forces upon the Czechoslovak republic. In peacetimes, it was under the competency and authority of the republics which from their own national budgets funded the procurement of the weapons and other capabilities required by the Territorial Defence should a state of war be imposed upon Yugoslavia. The Territorial Defence commander was appointed by the Presidency of Yugoslavia but always on the basis of consultation with the republic's authorities. General Hocevar was appointed in -- was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Territorial Defence, however, without any approval of the Republic of Slovenia which otherwise was provided for by law. When I was informed from the municipalities that the Territorial Defence's weapons were withdrawn from them, I asked General Hocevar to explain the situation. He said, "We are in fact replacing the old trophy weapons with state-of-the-art weaponry." Since this went on, I insisted on meeting with him, and what he said was the following: "In fact, I have received, he said, instructions that neither you nor anyone else from the leadership of Slovenia were to be informed about this activity, and that he has -- he found himself in a situation in which he's not quite clear whose orders to follow and that he will simply follow this order because he's supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now turn to tab 2 of Exhibit 447.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber has a translation, or a transcript and translation of this speech, but there is a difference between that improved version and the version that may be shown up on the screen. It's -- beg your pardon, it's tab 6. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, tab 6. Before we play this, this, I think, is an address in or about June 1990 of the accused at the Serbian parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The president of the Presidency of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, addressed the deputies of the parliament of Serbia with these words, explaining the draft version of the most important republican document. According to the new constitution, a unified Serbia was to be established as a sovereign state." The interpreters apologise but the tone is incomprehensible of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, the transcript that you have being available, I think the best course is for me to read out from the English, and the witness has heard the tape played yesterday in circumstances where it could be listened to and I think he recollected it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since we have it in front of us and time is short, if you would take the matters you rely on particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If we go down from where we are, the summarising passage by the journalist says that: "... the new constitution, the unique Serbia is to be established as a sovereign state..." Next sentence: "Stressing that the federal Yugoslavia is the main political choice for Serbia but with regard to strongly expressed disintegration and confederation tendencies in some parts of the country, Milosevic said: This is why this draft constitution of Serbia has been prepared respecting other possible options of Serbia as an independent state; passing the new constitution, among other things, should prevent every attempt of silent conversion of federal Yugoslavia into confederation, i.e., it represent a moment when Serbia is to clearly and on time say that the Serbia's administrative borders are linked only with the federal system in Yugoslavia because, should the system in Yugoslavia change, i.e., should there be a confederalisation, all the constitutional issues would be opened. A confederation is not a state but a union of independent states. Therefore, there is no confederation even if all the political subjects of Yugoslavia want it within the existing administratively set borders among the republics. In that case, in the case that they do not want the federal Yugoslavia, the issues of borders of Serbia is an open political issue." Further comments by the journalist, and then the accused speaks on the second page: "Therefore, because of the significance and because of the far-reaching consequences of fulfilment of the projects of political reform in Serbia and in interest in stable political conditions in Serbia, I suggest that the citizens express their views about the draft of the Presidency of Serbia through a referendum first. In that way, we would simply eliminate unnecessary conflicts and deprive the coalition, which acts against Serbia, from any basis for accusations that we want to impose the new constitution in a non-democratic way. Today especially when anti-Serb coalition leads to an unprecedented campaign against Serbia in the country and abroad and when in Kosovo yet another pitiful show is taking place whose playscript gets even the parliament of the region involved. Pulling in the highest organs of the government in the region in a non-constitutional and illegal way in the fight for Albanian separatists' causes in the name of democracy is the best proof that so-called Albanian Democratic Alternative is nothing else but nationalist movement for the separation of Kosovo and Metohija, i.e., a movement against the Serbian state and its integrity. Therefore, from this place I would like to say that the Serbian state will consider every attempt of seizing its territory to be an act against the state and the people and will act accordingly." Mr. Kucan, you saw this tape yesterday in circumstances where the sound was audible. We see what is said by the accused there about the borders being potentially an open issue. Remembering, please, that we are very pressed for time and if you could put it very summarily, what was the meaning, as you understood it, of this speech and what was its effect on you and others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, this is footage from a meeting of the Presidency of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia where they discuss the proposal of the Presidency of Serbia for a new constitution of the Republic of Serbia. This took place at a time in which in Yugoslavia we all sought for ways and means to resolve the crisis. At that time, different concepts were in the offing. We in Slovenia, throughout this period, advocated either a new agreement concerning the concept of the future state of Yugoslavia on the basis on establishing the interest to live in a single state, what are the interests and how to put them into practice. Once we noted that there is no such interest, we offered a variety of options. One of them was the possibility to establish a confederation comprising the republics of the former Yugoslavia. This proposal or draft Serbian constitution, which I think was adopted in the fall of 1990, in fact speaks about the understanding of a confederation by the political leadership in Serbia. It states that a confederation is not a state, and it also emphasises that they could not adopt this option since the political issue and question of the borders between the republics could arise. The point of departure in this matter was the following: The borders between -- of the republics in Yugoslavia are supposed to be administrative borders, which is contrary to facts. The first constitution after the Second World War outlined the borders. The borders were drawn on the basis of a consensus, and from that point onward, all Yugoslav constitutions included a provision that the borders between the republics cannot be changed without consensus of all the republics. Now, how I understand this message, as you've asked me, sir, let me answer in the following way: The message was that should Yugoslavia fall apart and should other forms be opted for, such as a confrontation, Serbia will never agree to a situation in which parts of the Serbian people living outside the territory of the Republic of Serbia be left beyond the Serb republic. This is the difference in concepts that I referred to in my introductory statements. Our understanding of the Yugoslav state differed, on our decisions consequently differed. However, let me emphasise that this is an approach through which Serbia, given the circumstances such as they were, tried to resolve the Serbian national question. This is, of course, a very difficult question to resolve. The alternative would have been to use the European standards and criteria, to use the international standards and criteria to safeguard and protect the rights of ethnic Serbs living as minorities in other republics throughout Yugoslavia, particularly in the Republic of Croatia as well as in the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the latter, the Serbs were one of the three constitutive peoples in the republic. As the Serb political doctrine emphasised throughout this period that Serbs cannot live as an ethnic minority in any part of Yugoslavia, this approach was a sort of a logical philosophical continuation of this doctrine. But it may also have implied that borders might be redrawn by use of force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may it be acceptable if I take another half an hour, and I hope no more with this witness. That will mean that I will have taken something in the region of two hours and I hope leave enough time in the remainder of the morning for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that. Mr. Kucan, I should say we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you remember, please, during the adjournment not to speak to anyone about your evidence until it's over. That's a direction we give to all witnesses. Could you be back in 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you can have the extra half an hour now. We may, as a result, have to sit rather longer into the adjournment period, but we can do that, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, I'll deal with some matters in brief because there's no need for us to deal with them extensively. Paragraph 36 of the court summary. The plebiscite you've already referred to in December with very large figures in favour of having an independent state, that decision to take place six months later, as I think you've already told us. Just yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 39 and 40 of the court summary. You're aware from passages in Jovic's published diary of the possibility of meetings between Kadijevic and Milosevic, closed meetings between Kadijevic, Milosevic, and Jovic dealing with military matters. Were you aware - just yes or no again - of those meetings at the time or did it only come to light when you read the book or learnt about it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No, I did not know about them then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 41. Did Slovenia and Croatia at this time or about this time favour the notion of a confederation of states, something that was rejected at a Presidency meeting in January 1991 which was attended by republican authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. In summer of 1990 at the Presidency of Yugoslavia, a decision was made that Slovenia and Croatia should elaborate such a draft contract and the rest of the four republics a modern confederation concept. However, this concept, this idea was rejected at the following session of the Presidency in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 42. Were there talks between Serb and Slovenian delegations in January of 1991 where you headed the Slovenian delegation and the accused headed the Serbian delegation where this confederation was discussed; and then in February were there meetings of the republican presidents in Belgrade, again consideration of confederation, confederal system, again rejected by Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia; and as a result of that, did you come to the view that the notion of a confederal model was not going to be accepted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: On the plebiscite on Slovenia's independence was adopted on December 23rd in 1990, and the results were proclaimed on the 26th of December, when the documents were also made public. And there are two characteristics to these documents that I wish to underscore. First, that Slovenia wishes to settle all relations with other republics once its independent, wishes to do so by consensus and wishes also to establish what the possibilities are for the future institutional cooperation with the republics of Yugoslavia. And a second feature of the documents then published after the plebiscite and around the plebiscite was the following; namely, that it will be the Assembly and the -- the Assembly and the government that will have to carry out all the necessary acts and measures necessary for Slovenia to become an independent state and basing this decision of theirs on the constitution and other legal documents of the Republic of Slovenia. And the Slovene political leadership then also decided as regards their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. intentions about the mode of independence and ways of regulating relations with other republics to do so in direct contact and talks with the leaderships of other republics and do so also at the meeting of federal bodies that we only saw as mediators between the republics and provinces. Our stand was that the constituent parts of Yugoslavia are the republics of the federation. Hence, the meeting that I had already mentioned, the 10th of January, 1991, when this bilateral meeting was held between the leadership of Slovenia and the leadership of Serbia. And the delegations at this meeting -- well, I was present there as well as the accused, and we could establish there that this was the end of this concept of transforming Yugoslavia into a confederation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we move towards the time when independence of Slovenia was to be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly request you to slow the witness down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down a bit, Mr. Kucan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we approach the time when independence of Slovenia was declared, we note that Croatia had announced an intention to declare independence at the same time and that there was then a meeting in Brdo on the 11th of April of 1991, in the process of continuing discussions and negotiations. Paragraph 45 of the summary. In the course of that meeting and during a break, did you go for a walk alone with the accused, talking about the difficulties and frustrations of that meeting, and can you tell us, please, in summary, what it was the accused said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. This meeting did take place, and it was one of the meetings that were regularly held. After January 1991, regular -- regular meetings of presidents of Yugoslav republics to discuss, in fact, just one topic, what a possible way out of the crisis is and also how to reshape living in Yugoslavia and the co-existing in Yugoslavia and whether a formula could be found for the future. And this particular meeting that was held at Brdo near Ljubljana was one such meeting, and at this meeting this is indeed also one of the questions that was discussed. And I did say that 26 months between the decision at the plebiscite and before independence was running out and that this discussion should become much more concrete. President Tudjman also said at the meeting that should Slovenia do so, the very same day Croatia was going to act accordingly and do the same. And we did discuss this with the accused at the -- when we took this walk together, and also after that, the accused said to me, "Well, if the Slovenes really want to leave the federation, well, in that case it will not be possible for us to be opposed to it," he said. "However, the conditions will have to be met before Slovenia can leave Yugoslavia. However, the same could not go for Croatia in view of the fact that a good portion -- number of Serbs were living on the territory of Croatia and in this way they are -- they really have this blood link, blood ties with Croatia." And when we heard this proposal about the Serb constitution in the tape and when it was said that it was not possible to accept any other form of relations between the republics in Yugoslavia than the federation, because otherwise all different questions are open, including also the borders of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 49 in the summary. Slovenia's independence was declared publicly on the 25th of June of 1991. I think you made the point that all documents were published and open for consideration, and I think there was inevitably some celebration on the day or the night of independence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of June, the Slovene Assembly adopted the documents, the fundamental charter on Slovenia's independence, then also a constitutional law to implement it as well as the independence declaration stating again what I have been trying to say all along, namely that Slovenia took this decision to exercise its right to self-determination but does not wish to do so at the detriment or against the right of any other nation in Yugoslavia, that it also wishes to settle all relations from the past and for the future as well as agree on forms of cooperation in the future. And these documents were published the following day, on the 26th of June, and it is then on that evening that this was celebrated and this was the sanctioned decision taken by the citizens of Slovenia concerning the autonomy and the independence of the Slovene state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We know of the short conflict, military conflict, between Slovenia and the JNA. Tell us when that started and when it finished, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, the JNA carried out this aggression immediately in the course of or after the celebration of independence. If my memory serves me right, that was 2.30 or 2:00 p.m. that night with the tanks that came out of the barracks on the way to the external borders of the republic of Slovenia. And this decision, so it seems, although we knew nothing about it, was adopted at a meeting of the federal government, but we considered it illegal and unconstitutional because only the Presidency of Yugoslavia could actually take such decisions, and this conflict or aggression or war on Slovenia then was first of all interrupted and then came to an end on the 7th of July with -- talks then were organised on the Brioni islands upon the proposal of the ministerial Troika of the European Union, and during the period of the 27th of June to the 7th of July made interventions within the framework of these armed conflict, and it is Hans van den Broek, the then Foreign Minister of the Netherlands that led the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia, please. When it happened, what did you notice about where the JNA withdrew to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The decision on the JNA's or the rest of the army's withdrawal, there were no longer Slovenes or Croats in JNA or members of other nations. This decision was adopted at the federal Presidency's meeting on the 18th of July, the first ten days after the Brioni meeting, that is. And the Presidency decided to ensure this withdrawal within a period of three months, and the last soldier left the Slovene territory on the 26th of October the same year. Now, among the documents that were adopted by the Assembly of Slovenia on the 26th of June, well, the period that was decided upon was five years to start with. However, then the Presidency decided that it would just be three months. The JNA did not withdraw to elsewhere in Slovenia or Croatia but mainly to Bosnia-Herzegovina and especially the territories with the majority -- which was majority -- with a Serb majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In Exhibit 448, the extracts from Jovic's diary, there are entries that you have reviewed on page numbered 311 at the foot for the 5th of July, and I'm going to just touch them rather than go through them because of the time. The 5th of July which begins with Jovic saying, "Slobodan and I scheduled a meeting with Kadijevic which we regard as critical. The situation in the country is almost tragic. The JNA has been defeated and routed in Slovenia. Army morale has hit rock bottom." Matters of that sort. We go over the page, in fact over two pages to the 15th of July on page 326: "We finally adopted a decision on withdrawing the JNA from Slovenia. Formally the decision states the JNA units from Slovenia will be redeployed to new positions," and so on. And then the 30th of July: "Veljko, Slobodan and I are sitting in my office before the Presidency with the presidents of the republics and the future of Yugoslavia." Next paragraph: "The JNA should be transformed into a military force of those who want to remain in Yugoslavia." We are very pressed for time now, Mr. Kucan. You've reviewed those entries. Anything you particularly want to refer to in them? Do they reflect, although you may not have known it at times, what you understand was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Except for the meeting of the Presidency that I mentioned, I said the 17th of July, it was the 15th of July. We did not have information about this meeting, but withdrawal to the positions to which the JNA withdrew from Slovenia confirms actually what we find in these notes as to the reasons why they go there and what their tasks is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you also reviewed passages in a book by Kadijevic, which we haven't yet exhibited but will become a separate exhibit, if it may, please. The same terms.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecution Exhibit 449.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without looking at the extracts, in order to save time, if you can deal with this, Mr. Kucan, what's your view on how Kadijevic describes the process of nationalisation of the army following its withdrawal from Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Which extract is this, please? If you're referring to the book --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The book. When the book was published, I read it, so what would you like to know exactly in connection with this book?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any immediate recollection of any particular passage dealing with the withdrawal of the army? I'll withdraw that question for the time being. It can possibly be raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, if you are referring to those excerpts and their description and his thoughts as to where the army should withdraw and what it should Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be done, obviously this is true, because it was part of the recognition that Yugoslavia no longer can be kept together. The army had been an integrating factor. Now with the withdrawal from Slovenia, its strategic mission changed. Not to protect and safeguard Yugoslavia but, rather, to protect the smaller Yugoslav borders, particularly the parts inhabited by ethnic Serbs. In fact, how I understand it is that apparently they do not want, or he doesn't want to, agree to parts of ethnic Serbs living outside a single state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours may want to have an eye on this extract on page 73 at the foot in particular and towards the foot, and the witness may wish to recall that there's reference in the book by Kadijevic to the Karlobag-Virovitica lines and thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any comment to make on what has been said about those lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as to where would be the borders of the limited Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia without Slovenia and parts of Croatia inhabited predominantly by ethnic Serbs, well, these do coincide with this line Virovitica-Karlovac further down to the south of Herzegovina and Montenegro. This had been spoken about in Yugoslavia quite often before and afterwards, and in fact, this book by Kadijevic simply confirms the reasoning that we had known from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other matter of fact, two other matters of commentary before I finish. The matter of fact I didn't deal with, it's at paragraph 14 of the summary. It goes back in time. In the build-up to the decision to secede or to have independence, did you have limitations on the information you received from the army? Did Slovenia suffer limitations in what it was told by the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: As far as the relationship between Slovenia and the JNA goes, this was characterised by a series of conflicts from 1988 onwards. The events that I'm sure the Chamber is fully familiar with. Therefore, it is quite understandable that we either had received no information from the JNA or we received very scattered information, particularly as far as their position and plans for Slovenia. We did know, however, that a special staff had been established to regulate the situation in Slovenia. This is what we have been told by the Slovene generals. However, we had no possibility whatsoever to verify this and check this at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two exhibits I haven't touched, tabs 4 and 5, being articles where this witness was interviewed in 1992 and 1993. The purpose of them, and they can be seen from the extracts included, that the phrase "Greater Serbia" was in use at the time even if not used by the accused. It was used as reflecting the ideas that were going on so far as Serbia was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My two conceptual questions that I want you to deal with in about one minute or two minutes each. As the -- paragraph 61. You take the view, I think, Mr. Kucan, that there were different values of what Yugoslavia should become after its break-up, and you take a view as to how it was that nationalism came to play a part. Could you express that, but really, I'm afraid, very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: In my introduction, I emphasised that one of the typical features of the crisis in Yugoslavia was also a crisis of values, ethical and others, and that in fact Yugoslavia as a non-aligned state and such as it had been had performed its role. Once the values, the system of values fell apart, it was the nationalist concept that had become the single criterion of any action and activity which by itself and in itself is not a tragic development. The desire and aspiration for freedom and independence by a people is a legitimate right. However, the question is whether this right can be exercised at the detriment of other people's rights, and this is where one of the major conceptual differences lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you take any view about how there was an absence of values, or a vacuum, indeed, that needed to be filled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, our proposals made at the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, i.e., the proposals made by the Slovene delegation, in fact were emphasising the need to fill this vacuum out with a new system of values and standards which Yugoslavia or, rather, Europe had been promoting since the Second World War, and I'm referring to Europe that had -- stood for the values such as democracy, open market economy, openness towards the world, and the need to safeguard the image that Yugoslavia had had internationally. I should also like to emphasise the following: Officially, "Greater Serbia" is not a term that had been used by the Serbian leadership, but the Republic of Serbia per se and the Republic of Serbia including all ethnic Serbians of course makes a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke earlier of the two concepts of Yugoslavia, one as the vehicle where all Serbs lived under one roof, the other as a community -- as nations in a community. The break-up, did it reflect one or other of those concepts, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The manner in which the concepts were implemented as well as the facts that took place in fact speak for themselves, and they are now shown today very vividly in the concepts that have been pursued by the current parts of the former Yugoslavia, and it is now obvious which parts are living under circumstances and values and standards that are characteristic of modern Europe, of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, at paragraph 62, do you feel it important to compare the break-up of the former Yugoslavia with the break-up of other territories into constituent parts at the same time or similar time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: By all means. This is very important for at least two reasons. Number one, our proposal also to the international community as well as to the European Union to realise and recognise that Yugoslavia's days were over and that their intervention is needed for this break-up to be controlled and free of violence. The second reason is closely associated with the first one. The response to our requests and proposals always was: Yugoslavia cannot be broken up because this would be a very bad model for the Soviet Union, and the Soviet Union is a much more complex case than Yugoslavia. In these changes and restructuring after the fall of the Berlin Wall, when the former Czechoslovakia fell apart, the Soviet Union fell apart and both these states fell apart on the basis of an agreement, peacefully, without the use of violence and without bloodshed. In a tragic and bloody manner, it was only Yugoslavia that broke up. The question, the crucial question, is why this took place and why did it happen in Yugoslavia alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There will be further questions from the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm not quite sure how much time you're going to give me for the cross-examination of this witness, because I can see that it's already after half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to give you the same as the Prosecution. That will be one hour, 50 minutes. We might extend that, if you don't waste time, to two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that's too short a time, but that is your -- the practice you have applied here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is only available today. We must get through his evidence and we must do so as equitably as we can. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to ask your indulgence for a minute of explanation by me. As the amicus throughout all this time, I have truly endeavoured to save as much time as possible. I think that I can say on behalf of the amicus that to bring in a key witness of this nature for only one day is not sufficient. I don't think it is enough time for us to get through everything that is necessary. I shall abide and respect your decision with regard to the time allotted for cross-examination, but I fear that we're going to find ourselves in a situation in which I will have no time to ask the witness anything, whereas I have very many key questions and issues to raise. So I should like to know how much time I can count on, as the amicus, for my questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have in this trial, as in any trial, to balance the need for evidence with the availability of witnesses, and in that availability we have to consider the convenience and the possibility of witnesses coming. That's one thing to bear in mind. Secondly, with respect to the amicus, of course you have an important role to fulfil, but it's more important that the time is taken up with cross-examination by the accused, and he should have his allotted time. As you've heard, there may be extra time this afternoon, and we'll consider whether it would be possible to fit as much as possible of your cross-examination in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just be allowed to add, I don't understand, although I do respect the work obligations of Mr. Kucan, however, witnesses of this kind, key witnesses, might I say, are brought into the courtroom for only one day, and I think that we ought to extend a caution to the Prosecution to ask them to find enough time, and I think every man in his life has enough time to spare, so that people can come in and have longer time with the witnesses. So that is the objection and remark I have to make on behalf of the amicus. That's something we'll have to weigh up and assess. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must get on now with the examination and not take up further time. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.
