utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we were saying, it's 25 minutes to 12:00 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask a preliminary question first. You mentioned the war in Slovenia. You used three expressions; "conflict," "aggression," and "war." Did Serbia have anything at all to do with that war in Slovenia which, as you said, went on for ten days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, I used the expression "the war in Slovenia." I apologise. A war against Slovenia. Slovenia was confronted with JNA. Who influenced the acts of the JNA can be judged today on the basis of the documents which are at the disposal of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At that time, and I hope you also know today, that we in Serbia didn't know about that intervention at all when it began. We had no idea, and we couldn't have known in advance when we didn't know when it actually began.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Distinguished Your Honours, we in Slovenia turned to the federal bodies, believing that the federal bodies were controlling the JNA, and the federation was the sole other party in this dialogue between the two. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But that -- does that then mean that Serbia has nothing to do with the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I do not know. Documents speak about that, as well as books which had been written later. My conclusions today on the basis of facts that I know today I didn't -- and which I didn't know at the time they were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you know, it would be much easier and much more productive to deal with what the witness himself knew and what he dealt with, and what he said about this is that he doesn't know at the time whether Serbia was involved. He dealt with the federal authorities. Now, what I caution you against, Mr. Milosevic, because it wastes time, is getting into arguments with witnesses, dealing with things which they haven't come to give evidence about. His conclusions are not relevant what -- unless they affected what happened at the time. His conclusions about the evidence are subject to what this Trial Chamber is going to find. We're going to make conclusions about what the evidence is insofar as it's relevant to this indictment. So there's not much point asking him about his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking him about his conclusions. What I'm asking him is about his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have the transcript from the meeting of the 21st of August, and I'm going to read out the first sentence and one sentence later on. "'I am not going to be responsible,' says Milan Kucan: 'I'm not going to be responsible to the Prime Minister who quite obviously, now that he has lost the war, wants to win everything else,'" and so on and so forth. And then there's another sentence. In speaking about the fact that the two members of the federal government who had left would not be returning, you go on to say: "I don't have to convince you that you're not going to find a man in Slovenia, including these two men, who will return to the federal government and work in it. That is the SIV, the federal government for which we know in Slovenia started the war in Slovenia." And those are your very words. Have I quoted you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes, and it's clear that Slovenia acted in this way, and that was also my stand in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which year are we talking about and what were the circumstances of the meeting? Which meeting was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a meeting of the Presidency of the SFRY in extended composition, as was the term used at the time, which meant that those present -- we were present, the presidents of the Presidencies or the presidents of the republics, the individual Yugoslav republics. I attended the meeting and so did the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And which year?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- it was on the 21st of August, 1991, after the conflict in Slovenia. And therefore this observation made by the witness, which quite clearly speaks about who did what at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let's dwell for a moment on some more serious matters because these are things you have talked about. I think they're essential. Was it clear that the federal organs, as you yourself state, undertook individual measures and took steps to make it impossible to infringe upon the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the SFRY? Was that the explanation that was given at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Slovenia was not infringing upon the territorial integrity of SFR Yugoslavia. It was -- in a legitimate way it was availing itself of its right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the very next day, that is to say after the proclamation of the independence of Slovenia on the 25th of June, already on the 26th of June, the day after, you took control of the borders, took down all the plaques which said "Yugoslavia" on it at the border crossings, that you took over the customs control, customs offices and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: In line with the decisions of the republican Assembly, after proclaiming its independence, it effectively took over the authority on the border and carried out these operations mentioned by the accused and put up the border plaques with the name of Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the activities that were taken by the federal government were reactions to what had in fact taken place. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, six months after the plebiscite and the announcement that the decision of the plebiscite would be implemented in six months, there were no other reactions with which we would resolve the situation after the independence of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember the statements made by the US State Secretary, the Secretary for Foreign Affairs, on the 12th of January, 1995, in the American Senate, that the war was started by Slovenia? Do you know about that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I know also of similar statements, and I don't deny the right of anyone to have his own opinion on what has been happening in Yugoslavia, but of course I have a right to my own opinion, which I have also stated in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about an opinion. I'm talking about facts. And do you happen to remember, Warren Zimmermann wrote this, the last American ambassador to the SFRY, in a journal called Foreign Affairs, the March/April issue 1991, the title is "Remembering the Catastrophe in Yugoslavia," and he writes the following: "Contrary to generally held opinions, the Slovenes were the ones who started the war. Their declaration of independence, which was not preceded by any efforts to negotiate, really did place under their control all border crossings between Slovenia and its two neighbours Italy and Austria. This meant that Slovenia was the sole international passage between the Western Yugoslavia and that it appropriated the right and goods intended for other countries and the revenues from customs taxes which amounted to 75 per cent of the national budget. Even a less primitive army than the JNA would have reacted. The worst thing of all was the understandable wish of the Slovenes to be independent, however, condemned the rest of Yugoslavia for war." And that was verbatim a quotation by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- just a moment. You read that out. The witness should have a chance to comment on it, part by part. Mr. Kucan, you've dealt with the point about whether the Slovenes started the war. What's said is there was no effort to negotiate beforehand, and the effect was that Slovenia was the international passage, as it's put, between Yugoslavia and that you appropriated various rights in connection with customs and the like, so the JNA was bound to react. You've probably heard this, these sort of comments before, but obviously you should have the chance of responding to them since the accused has put them to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the position of the former Ambassador Zimmerman of the United States. I am acquainted with that. There are also other and different opinions from that. Of course the assertion doesn't stand that Slovenia did not -- did nothing in order to assure that this would take place in a peaceful and orderly manner. Already at the meeting in January, in January 1991, after the meetings when it turned out that no agreement could be achieved about the reorganisation of Yugoslavia, our Assembly, the Assembly in February 1991 adopted a declaration on an agreed upon disassociation with a proposal, which contained a proposal how to ensure Slovene self-determination where it was also stated that it doesn't want it any other way than through an agreement with other republics. This declaration had been then sent to all the Assemblies of other republics and provinces. The only answer and positive answer we received was from the Assembly of Croatia. No other answer received. So this was just one of the examples what Slovenia did in order to assure that this would happen in agreement and in a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, I hope we're not challenging the fact that nobody in Yugoslavia disputed the right of Slovenia to self-determination, the right of the Slovenian people to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who, then, did challenge the right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: There is -- was a difference between the principled view, stand, and the practical stand, namely that this right can be implemented up to the right of secession or that the federal bodies determined that. While in the federal bodies you had a majority decision-making. We know what that looked like at the Congress, the 14th Congress in January, 1991, when Slovenia came with its legitimate and rightful proposals and through which it was brutally outvoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you comment on the passage that Mr. Milosevic quoted to the effect that one result of your declaration of independence was that you had the right to impose customs duties on goods coming into Western Yugoslavia. I'm not sure I quite understand that. Was that a consequence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the decisions of the Slovene Assemblies was to take over the customs duties, customs duties which were taxed on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia. It would have been paid into a special fund and then the decision concerning this fund would be taken during the talks on the future. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean the decision as to how the funds would be distributed among the other republics. I see. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was also specified in the Brioni accord Annex 1. It was July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: July 1991. The Brioni agreement was after the war and here we're talking about the war. So tell me, as you did have the possibility of stepping down from Yugoslavia in the way Slovakia did, for example, and you opted for violence and you played the decisive role, and of course Germany, Austria, the politicians that you discussed this issue with, why then did you opt for war when you could have stepped down peacefully? Why did you attack the JNA in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The decision concerning the customs and the fate of the customs was a decision adopted by the Slovene Assembly on the 25th of June. And as far as other countries and politicians from other countries, I cannot involve them concerning the Slovene decision. The decision was taken by us. We weren't influenced by anybody else. The risk we took upon ourselves. As far as Slovakia is concerned, nobody set any conditions. It was an agreement which was reached by the two presidents of the Czech and the Slovak government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned the fact that you weren't able to go to the federal organs not to be outvoted, to avoid being outvoted. I think you know that in the Federal Assembly, according to the constitution, nobody could be outvoted and that the federal council and the council of chambers and provinces existed at the time, so Slovenia could not have been outvoted on an issue of this kind. A consensus was being offered. So bearing this in mind, why, then, did you attack the JNA on your territory, the JNA which went there to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer one question at a time. The question was that you were being offered, it's said, a consensus. Would that be true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The law on secession as was proposed would have been adopted in the federal chamber, not in the chamber of republics and provinces where consensus was needed. It was the federal chamber where the majority vote prevailed. And also, the Serbian leadership, when speaking of greater efficiency of the federal bodies, they also insisted one man, one vote, and it meant that for the smaller nations within the federation, we'd be outvoted. So this assertion doesn't stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is precisely the fact that this law was not adopted because of a lack of consensus confirms that the assertion does stand, because the law was not adopted because they could not agree on the basis of a consensus. Isn't that so, Mr. Kucan? Why wasn't the law adopted, then, if we had the majority in the Assembly, and those four other republics, and were able in the federal chamber to adopt it by a majority a vote? It wasn't adopted, wasn't passed because there was no consensus. You did not allow it to be adopted, in fact, and to step down peacefully as a result.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be difficult for me -- as a member of a small nation, it would be difficult for me to dictate to the majority. It was another matter was at stake. Was it a decision, Slovene decision of secession or issue of disassociation from Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia wouldn't exist without Slovenia. We were a constitutive element of Yugoslavia. And this has roots in 1918 when the country was founded and what it is. That is why we proposed this concept of disassociation and the declaration of the Republican Assembly in February 1991, it proposed it to the assemblies of the other republics to reflect and reconsider it. I know also of many other proposals concerning -- and drafts of this law on secession, and there were two lines of thinking, the indissolubility of the republics concerning all the debts of all the individual republics, so how much each and every republic borrowed abroad for its development, and it would be requested that the -- it would also request that its workers be employed also in all other republics. So these were the thinkings along the lines concerning this draft law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely why I'm asking you this, because you yourself said a moment ago the right to self-determination, which is the right enjoyed by all nations, all ethnic groups, and that that could not be realised at the expense of the same rights enjoyed by others. So is that clear? Do we agree on that point at least?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: As far as the fact that each nation has the right to self-determination, yes, they all. But it's not an abstract category. It lives in a reality, and it is linked to the republic in the context of the border, because the borders between the republics were borders and borders that cannot be changed without the agreement of the affected republic. Therefore, the decision of self-determination was fixed on the territory and not the changes of territories. We have not tried to infringe upon the territories either of the other republics of Yugoslavia or of other neighbouring countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the intervention of the federal government wasn't on inter-republican borders but on the external borders of Yugoslavia which it was its constitutional right to do, wasn't it? And you attacked the army on your territory. The Yugoslav People's Army, the only legitimate army in Yugoslavia at that time, and you attacked it on your territory, which took up positions on the external borders of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: For many years, Your Honours, I had this unpleasant duty to carry on the political debates on what Yugoslavia is. The external borders of Yugoslavia were also Slovene borders. And when Slovenia decided to go independent legally, all Slovene borders became external borders. And as I said before, there can be no Yugoslavia without Slovenia, so there was no need to defend the Yugoslav borders, at least not there where Slovenia was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Obviously this is changing the subject, because I quoted Zimmerman who is giving the exact reasons why you did that. But to be practical, let us move on. Do you please remember your involvement on NTV television, one of those private TV stations in 1995, in November, together with Mesic, Tomac, Spegelj in a live programme? Do you remember that programme that you were a participant of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I would have to look at the footage. I would have to look at the footage; we had many such programmes, I don't know exactly which you're thinking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember, I'm referring to the programme aired on the 8th of November, on the NTV private TV station in which you participated together with Stipe Mesic who at the time headed the party of Croatian Independent Democrats, and also participating were Spegelj, Tomac and others. It was a Kontakt programme. Spectators called in and you had a lot of discussion. I'm sure you didn't have many programmes with the same participants, especially on that date and that year, so surely you remember that programme.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do remember the programme but I don't remember the date, and of course I don't have such a memory to recollect both the programmes and the dates, but I do remember participating in the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's fine. Now, do you remember that in that programme Mesic - you were present - declared, Mesic declared, that the former Minister of Foreign Affairs of Germany, Hans Dietrich Genscher, and the Pope John Paul II, by the direct agreement and support designed to break up the former Yugoslavia had practically contributed most to that actually happening? Do you remember the positions he took and the explanations he gave along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Those were the stance of Mr. Mesic. I already mentioned before that foreign statesmen will not be involved in this story of the independence of Slovenia. Also, in connection with the concrete name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, let us just stick to whatever it is the accused wants to put. That is what Mr. Mesic said, something along those lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But my experience with these people is different. That is what I wanted to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean with reference to Genscher and the Pope?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm asking you whether Mesic said what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you exactly want from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Kucan. You are testifying here. Among other things, half of your testimony referred to the book by Borisav Jovic. So I'm now asking you, for instance, about a statement by Stipe Mesic in front of you in a Kontakt programme in which you took part together. You said here that you could confirm here what Jovic said at meetings that you attended. Now I'm asking you whether you could confirm what Mesic said in a Kontakt programme you were in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Milosevic. The witness has agreed with that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just specify something else, please. Do you remember that at the time Mesic said that he came to Belgrade, to the highest position in the federation in order to, through the mediation of the Yugoslav diplomacy at the time, to get in touch with the most influential factors and to persuade them that the survival of Yugoslavia was nonsense? And I have a quotation: "I wanted to convey that the idea of the break-up of Yugoslavia to those who had the greatest influence on its fate, to Genscher and the Pope. In fact, I had three meetings with Genscher. He enabled a contact with the Holy See. The Pope and Genscher agreed with the total break-up of SFRY." Was that what he said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this programme which I participated together with Mr. Mesic, I can confirm that. But to be able to confirm each and every word, I'd need either a transcript or a video in order to be able to confirm it. These are very weighty words, and to testify like this wouldn't -- just wouldn't do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were these put to Mr. Mesic? I don't remember. Just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I do not recall these passages being put, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were not put because when I was cross-examining Mesic, I didn't have this information about that particular programme. Otherwise, I would have surely. But since Mr. Kucan was a participant, I think it is quite relevant to establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't remember the particular detail, and he's dealt with it generally. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Tomac at the time recalled that Slovenia and Croatia, as long as 1990, had formed a strong partnership in favour of the break-up of Yugoslavia? He was, according to his criteria, was favourable for you, and this tandem, this couple, consisted of Franjo Tudjman and yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I and nobody else from the leadership of Slovenia worked on the concept of the break-up of Yugoslavia. We only worked together on the reorganisation, restructuring of Yugoslavia. I mentioned the session of the Presidency in the summer of 1990 when it was agreed that Slovenia and Croatia prepare a concept of a federation, and also a confederal agreement was drawn up but which wasn't accepted by the other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Four republics, as you yourself said, did not agree to it. But then let us go back since I asked you why you attacked the Yugoslav People's Army when it wasn't jeopardising anyone over there. I'm asking you now, is it true that during the conflict in Slovenia 44 members of the JNA were killed, 184 seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must refute the assertion that -- the assertion that Slovenia attacked the JNA. It wasn't the Slovene army that went out of the barracks to attack the JNA, but it was the JNA, according to our judgement, on the basis of an illegal, unconstitutional decision of the federal government, moved out of the barracks not only in Slovenia but also those located on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. And that is a fact, and it's an unavoidable fact. In this war, in fact, regrettably, people died. According to our data, 37 members of the JNA, eight members of the Slovene TO, four policemen, six civilians, citizens of Slovenia, and six foreigners who were at the time on the territory -- our territory of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have here a list of the killed and wounded members of the JNA in Slovenia, and as I'm saying that this was an attack on the JNA, I should like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the worst kind of crimes that you committed against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we get there, let's deal with this. Where does the list come from which you want to tender into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an official book, "Killed and died members of the JNA," those who died from the consequences of their injuries, with their names, date of birth, garrison they belonged to. It's easily verifiable and is not at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just hand it in and we'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can do that later on, just to save time. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the worst kind of crimes you committed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Nice has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If this extract is admissible, then the whole book should be admitted, in our respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be more valuable. There may be issues as to whether it's admissible in any event because it may lack relevance, simply to put a list of names in light of the answer given by the witness. But if it is relevant, we would invite the accused to provide the whole book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we might do is this, we will hand you it to look at during the adjournment, which is just coming up. You can have a look at it, but what we might simply do is mark it for identification and it may become relevant in due course. But hand this, if you would, to the Prosecution and we'll consider it after the adjournment. We're going to adjourn now. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 135, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've reviewed it. We would not object to its being marked for identification. Obviously, we need to see the book in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please give me brief answers because our time is limited. Do you remember that at five crossing points you brought minor children of officers and, under threat of death, you forced them to call on their fathers to surrender? Right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No, we didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that armed civilians arrested JNA members in the streets of towns and then in prisons they were subjected to various kinds of torture, such as scheduling their execution and things like that? Do you remember that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that you expelled or evicted from their apartments the families of officers, threatening to liquidate them unless they left Slovenia within a certain time period, by a certain deadline?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the Territorial Defence of Slovenia, with so-called units of national protection, set up barricades to prevent the passage of the JNA? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the barricades were first put up by the citizens of Slovenia. The Territorial Defence wasn't organised yet. It was on the night from the 26th/27th of June when we -- the citizens were celebrating their independence, and when going home, they saw the tanks coming, and they put up -- they used their cars, the buses to place in front of these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have documentation in support of all this, so I won't dwell on it. You certainly remember that passenger vehicles with licence plates from Serbia, ordinary passengers, civilians, who happened to be on the territory of Slovenia had their cars seized from them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone. I'm sorry, the interpreter can't hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You certainly remember that passenger vehicles with licence plates from Serbia, various civilians who were travelling on business or otherwise, that their vehicles were seized and the passengers were held as hostages and used as human shields? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I took the oath to speak the truth, nothing but the truth, it's not possible to answer these questions. In Slovenia, due to the aggression of the JNA, some trucks were stopped and the drivers and passengers were warned that they could be attacked and were asked to withdraw. I allow that maybe in these columns of vehicles there could be some vehicles with Serbian licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the military hospital, the military hospital in Ljubljana and the rehabilitation centre in Rimska Toplica were blocked and electricity and water were cut off, as well as food supplies, and there were vehicles placed in front of them filled with gas and petrol cans? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: In order that they were brought trucks with gas cylinders, I don't know, but I know that civilians were also injured concerning civilian hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that these institutions, that is the military hospital and the military rehabilitation centre, were told that they would be destroyed, together with their patients, if the JNA undertakes any military actions in the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I do not know that, but I know that the JNA used helicopters to transport the injured and that they wore the sign of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that extending aid to wounded soldiers was prevented and that there were even attacks on ambulances, streets were blocked, the civilian medical service refused to extend first aid to officers and soldiers of the JNA due to which some very young soldiers died of wounds that were not lethal.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: From as far as I know, our civilian hospitals and first aid had the task to help each and every one who was injured, be it the JNA -- members of the JNA, the police, the TO, or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since that is not true, but I have documents in support of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness asserts that it is, so there's no point arguing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I will not argue, Mr. May. I don't want to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember injuries of civilians which shows that there was violence against the lives and health of individuals, that hostages were taken, that there was terrorism, that there were impermissible threats made? I have information. I'll just read out the title: "Violations of the Rules of International Humanitarian Law by Members of the Armed Forces of Slovenia."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is also from this white book. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Could this be also exhibited and then you will consider it, because I don't have time to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember violations of international law with respect to civilians, the injured, and patients and the dead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. This is another entry from the same book; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let us have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, different considerations might apply to this extract, seeing the way the title's been read, because if it's going to go in in any way as evidence of what it says, it's probably something we would object to, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The list can be marked for identification. It's no more than that. It appears to be an extract from the book. The Prosecution can make objections in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 136, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember violations of international law with respect to the civilian population, the wounded, the sick, dead persons, medical staff? I have here 19 such cases of failure to respect those rules, failure to respect medical staff, impermissible attacks on Red Cross marked vehicles and ambulances. This is violations of the rules regarding the sick, the wounded, the dead, et cetera. There are 19 different entries, and I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is merely some allegations which are made by somebody in a book, no doubt. You can call evidence about it in due course, but first of all, the witness should have the opportunity to deal with these allegations and suggestions. Mr. Kucan, it's alleged, as you've heard, that there were various violations of international law with respect to medical staff, attacks on Red Cross vehicles, and other violations about the sick and the wounded. Normally, I would have the accused go through these 19 allegations one by one, but in the interests of saving time, I'm not going to do that. But you should have the opportunity of answering. Is it true that there were violations on the Slovene side, of these rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these allegations, these types of allegations put forward by the accused I refute and in the most decided manner. This is a propaganda brochure which was published and printed by Narodna Armija. Slovenia, in connection with these cases mentioned by the accused, this has been investigated by the investigative judge, by a forensic expert, and we have documents on this which are preserved in the Ministry of Defence. And if the Court wishes so, it will be able to receive it. I assert that this was not -- was not happening in Slovenia. And even if something like this did happen, it would be an extreme, excessive situation. The TO members, the JNA, and also the civilians were here. But later, what was happening in Srebrenica, Vukovar, Dubrovnik, and the concentration camps, this was a system, and I don't believe that there the investigations have been completed as they have been in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. May, so you won't accept this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These injuries, violations of the rules?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 19 points? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember violations of the rules with respect to people in custody? I have 17 different entries proving that the wounded and the sick were not given appropriate aid but they were threatened, their lives were threatened, their human dignity violated, and so on. Is that incorrect too, Mr. Kucan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already answered to that. I said that we also offered assistance, and after the Brioni accord, it was also agreed that the exchange would take place of the POWs as well as of the injured, and so they could go wherever they wished to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you won't accept this either as an exhibit, Mr. May? Very well. I have here some documents which say, for instance, Vednost [phoen], which means for information of the president of Slovenia, Mr. Milan Kucan. These are documents of the District Court in Kopar [phoen] of the Helsinki Monitor of Slovenia, et cetera, signed the president, Neva Miklavcic Predan, the president of the Helsinki board of Slovenia. I have documents of the state Prosecutor's office in Maribor, et cetera, also forwarded to you for your attention. And the question is: Are you informed about the well-known case when three captured members of the JNA were executed? Three captured members of the JNA executed by Slovenian policemen at the Holmec crossing on the 28th of June, 1991. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The Holmec case and all the other cases mentioned in the white book have been investigated. As I said, a report exists of the findings, and the Court may also request it and receive it. But that there was no say of this that civilians or that POWs would be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't get the Serbian interpretation. I just heard you speaking, Mr. Kucan, but I think you said that they were not executed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly that as POWs, that they had been shot, then my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these three JNA members were not executed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I even have here the notes of the post-mortems, the reports on the post-mortems of these three JNA members who were executed. I have the letters of the Helsinki committee, and other documents. So would at least these documents be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness see them first of all. He may have a comment on them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can see all of them. But let me just first find something else. Yes, the Prosecutor's office. This whole set of documents as an exhibit, I would like the witness to look at it. I also have information that the opposite side has received such documents, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us with those, Mr. Kucan, what they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What does this prove? That -- it just goes to prove that Slovenia also in the case of war acted as a state with a rule of law, that the prosecution came in, carried out their investigation and made its findings. The Helsinki Monitor also was involved. I asserted that these soldiers were not killed and executed as prisoners of war, but unfortunately, they were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the, according to the accused, a file or part of a file which the Prosecutor's office had. Is that a correct way to describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the Prosecution has at its disposal, but these are authentic documents referring to the work of the judicial bodies of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this then, please; were these people executed or were they not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with it first of all by way of deciding whether to admit it or not. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All I would add for your deliberations is this: There is a threshold of relevance for consideration when we're looking at events in Slovenia. For Croatia, Bosnia, and Kosovo, of course there's a conflict, and therefore, what's done by the other side is raised as relevant by the accused. I'm not going to try and hold out any documents that may be helpful, but if we consider receiving the white book and then in consequence the whole report in answer to the white book which will add to the materials before the Chamber, we may have gone too far in broadening the admissibility of evidence, but it's a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit these documents. We bear in mind what the Prosecution say about relevance, but meanwhile, de bene esse, we'll admit these and allow the accused to cross-examine on these matters of detail. In due course we'll have to decide how relevant the matter is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I presented just a few examples from all that which show that in that alleged attack by the JNA and the aggression against Slovenia, the casualties were several times greater, several times more soldiers with the JNA, just eight members, in fact, of the Territorial Defence of Slovenia among them were killed, and this was exclusively self-defence from an attack, an attack which was not caused or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over all this. The witness has given his evidence. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. In the statement -- in his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement, actually, the witness in point 75 quotes Kostic and Jovic at Brioni Island, as it says here, and they say: "A few Slovenians hate Yugoslavia so much and wish to leave Yugoslavia, then okay, leave this country but don't kill our sons, because their mothers did not bear them to be killed and die on Slovenian territory." That is your own quotation. Now, why did you need this war at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- Slovenia didn't want this war. It didn't need this war, and it didn't initiate it. The sons of Serb -- of Montenegrin mothers died, but so did of Slovenian mothers, but certainly we did not, Slovenia did not instigate this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's now take a look at something. I presented some assertions. I don't think by mutual people, but those who weren't well disposed to Yugoslavia when the war began, actually. So is it true that you could have left Yugoslavia without a war and that you started a war in order to destroy the whole of Yugoslavia? That that was in fact your role?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Listen, the witness has said many times that they did not start the war. So any question which is based on that is irrelevant. Any question based on that sort of assertion. You've heard his answer. Now, let's move on to something else, some of the detail of his evidence which he actually gave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, his statement is a very lengthy one, Mr. May. It comprises 27 pages. We have different observations made throughout, and we have some short explanations too. So I have a great deal of questions to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You speak about the following: In point 6, paragraph 6, you say that the Serbs insisted upon the fact that Yugoslavia continued into existence due to an annexation of the other kingdom, which is correct, and why the Serbs said that Slovenia was seceding from Yugoslavia, and we insisted that it was dissociation. Do you agree, Mr. Kucan, quite a construed construction, because the Serbs considered that the Slovenes could, according to their own free will, decide about their own fate and destiny, but they cannot impose their will on others, by the same token, those who wish to remain living in Yugoslavia? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't like to reopen all the discussions concerning different views on the break-up of Yugoslavia and the role of Yugoslavia in the lives of these nations. It didn't come through annexation, it was the free will of everyone who united into Yugoslavia. I'm looking back at the year 1918. It's true that on our own free will we left. We didn't want to impose this on anyone. We took many actions - I won't list them all - to ensure that it would be done in a peaceful way and a way that we could all agree upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up a few points first, please. I'm sure you know enough to be able to do so and that you're competent to do so. You said that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were one of the three constituent peoples, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the referendum on the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina without one of the three constituent peoples, in this case the Serb people, could have been legitimate or not, was legitimate or not, judging by the criteria, principles, provisions of the Yugoslav constitution, general norms, and a question of principle as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness isn't here as a constitutional expert, and the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you call it, has not been put into issue by his evidence. So his opinion as to that will not assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a question of me asking him as a constitutional expert. I'm asking him with respect to his statement when he said that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were one of the three constituent peoples, and that isn't something that is challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me explain one thing: What's in his statement is not evidence. He's not given evidence about that. It's what he says here which is evidence. Now, as I say, time is short, and we're not going to be assisted by his views, with respect to him, on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well, Mr. May. I won't take everything he said into consideration, just in part, because I assume that the statement is a basis for asking legitimate questions, or a legitimate basis for questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said today here and now something about a meeting you had with the Presidency, the Yugoslavia state Presidency and the president of the Federal Executive Council, the SIV, and as you've said, and I made a note of that, you asked to complete the constitutional changes, amendments, that they be completed, that they should not insist that this process be stopped, and that your answer was that the Constitutional Court was in existence and that it there up to determine whether something was unconstitutional or not; is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You indicated the authority of the Constitutional Court as a form of guarantor, that the constitutional order would not be upset, infringed upon. However, as you speak about Slovenia's attachment to legality and democracy, is it true and correct that, in opposition to this, Slovenia, through unilateral decisions made by its state organs in fact was aiming at destroying the legal order by its representatives in the Yugoslav Assembly and made decisions which were not in conformity with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia itself? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: This is not accurate, because before the Constitutional Court there were four amendments, one speaking of the rights of religious communities to establish schools, then another one speaking of the fact that a state of emergency could not be declared without the agreement of the republic authorities, a third amendment speaking of linking up large technological systems, the post, the railway, and thirdly the exercise of this right to self-determination. Two constitutional judges in Yugoslavia, because each republic had two judges in the federal -- in the federal bodies, had each separate view on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about anybody's opinion during a meeting of the Constitutional Court, because everybody's entitled to their own opinion but it is the court that makes a ruling. You said today, and just confirm, that as a guarantee that everything would proceed in a constitutional manner, you mentioned the existence of the Constitutional Court which would act and assess whether something was constitutional or not, whereas in fact you were dealing with the toppling, you wanted to topple the constitutional order of Yugoslavia. And in connection with the witness's assertion along those lines, that he offered the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia as a guarantor, I have the authentic decisions by the Constitutional Court, which of course I won't have time to read through here and now because I would need several days to read through them, but they are authentic decisions, and we have here the opinions of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia with respect to amendments 9 to 90, amendments to the constitution and the constitution of Slovenia aligned with that of Yugoslavia. Furthermore, they're opinions that the amendments were contrary to the constitution in the field of national defence, another decision and ruling made by the Constitutional Court which the witness referred to in his talks and confirmed again today. Then furthermore, the Constitutional Court observes that the -- an amendment to the constitution of Slovenia was not in order, re paragraph 99 and Article 1, paragraph 1.2 on the law of putting a stop to certain crimes and offences, and the declaration on the sovereignty of the Republic of Slovenia. This was something that was annulled by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia and its decision with respect to articles 4 and 10 of the plebiscite law. Yes. I have been cautioned to speak more slowly for the interpreters. And then Article 4 and 10 of the law on plebiscite, as I said, the independence and autonomy of the Republic of Slovenia. This was also overruled by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia. Then there was another decision, the constitutionality and a proposal for disassociation of the socialist -- from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was overruled by the Constitutional Court. And then there was another decision overruling your proposals referring to defence and protection. That was overruled too. Then the decision to assess the military responsibilities, which also overruled, and articles 2, paragraph 2 of Article 3 and 4, and Articles 6, 7, and 8 of the law on amendments to the Safety on the Roads Act and the decision to determine the constitutionality of the constitutional charter referring to the independence and autonomy of the Republic of Slovenia. So these were Constitutional Court decisions and rulings. We have another one; the law to implement the basic constitutional charter on the independence and autonomy of the Republic of Slovenia. Another decision assessing the constitutionality of the declaration with respect to independence. The decision to assess the customs services and how far they were constitutional. And this was something that you brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because you've read out a great long list and the witness should have the opportunity of commenting, and indeed of answering, if necessary, individual decisions. Mr. Kucan, you've heard the accused refer to a number of decisions of the -- just a moment. Just a moment. -- of the Yugoslav Constitutional Court. If you want to look at any of them or you want to comment on any individually or as a whole, this will be your opportunity to do so, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These decisions, I'm aware of them. And the accused is saying that the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia quashed these acts, and the Constitutional Court did not have such an authority but could establish whether this was not in conformity and what the state of compliance with the constitution of Yugoslavia was. I wish to assert that this is very important, because just as all other cases of voting occurred in Yugoslavia, the same method was used in the Constitutional Court, and both judges, constitutional judges from Slovenia, in the case of these documents, had a view differing from those of the majority of other judges on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say the same method of voting, Mr. Kucan, what was that method of voting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, the one that was evident at the 14th session and that would also happen in the Federal Assembly, for instance; laws would be adopted if a decision was to be made on disassociation from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if we look at these decisions, we'll find the Slovene judges will be in a minority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, yes, they were on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us, we'll no doubt be able to find out, but can you tell us, did any other judges side with them or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to see it on the basis of concrete judgements or concrete rulings of the Constitutional Court, and I think that now just guessing this could mislead the Court, the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, I don't know where the sense of this is, comparing voting at party Congresses which, according to the rules of procedure as to who votes and that there should be a majority vote on the part of those present and Constitutional Court decisions which, according to its rules of procedure, at the level of laws makes decisions which cannot be adopted unless they have a qualified majority to do so. And any court in the world - supreme, constitutional, whatever - makes rulings on the basis of a majority vote. So are you saying -- let me be more precise and specific in answering -- asking my question: That the Constitutional Court overruling these acts of Slovenia, documents of Slovenia, or, rather, in which they express their view that they are unconstitutional and not in conformity with the constitution of Yugoslavia, were made -- decisions were made by violating the work of the Constitutional Court, or did the Constitutional Court work in keeping with its code of conduct and rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, you see the accused is saying that it is really irrelevant to present the mode of voting used. I think it is very important to point the voting out, because this was showing the majority of views, of stands of one republic through the voting mechanism and putting this minority or, concretely, the Republic of Slovenia in a position where it can never really assert its views and make them accepted. And this was one man, one vote, which obviously is a democratic principle. In a multinational country, there is this principle of one man, one voice, which would be replaced by one man, one republic, one vote and where no outvoting is possible but where consensus or agreement is the basis for decisions. In 1989, at the meeting that has already been referred to, I did point out this necessity for consensus, for agreement, and the answer that was given to me is that changes could not be achieved on this basis on the basis of consensus, and this is this logic which differs from the one that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, let's not put things upside down like this and reverse the thesis. What I'm talking about is legal decisions on the part of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia and not about one man, one vote, that system. You said yourself that you asked the Yugoslav state Presidency and the federal government at a meeting that you talked about this morning to complete your constitutional changes and that guarantees -- that you gave guarantees that this would not sidestep the constitution of Yugoslavia. And a Constitutional Court exists to rule if something is not in conformity with constitution. And once the Constitutional Court made its decisions, you say that this was to the detriment of your republic because the Constitutional Court ruled that you were unconstitutional in toppling the legal system of Yugoslavia. Is that what you're in fact saying, Mr. Kucan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the federal Constitutional Court did not say that Slovenia toppled the constitutional order of Yugoslavia. What I am saying is what would be the meaning of a constitutional decision that there be judges, an equal number of judges coming from each individual Yugoslav republic? And if I went -- if I had to conclude on this basis, I could say that both constitutional -- constitutional judges from Slovenia therefore could be considered as being incompetent and without having authority to participate in this decision-making if I were to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they did participate in the decision-making process, but if they are left in the minority, as you know, and the Constitutional Court meets in full composition in plenary session and therefore takes decisions on that basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Milosevic, we've taken this point as far as we can. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have too. So look at those 27 decisions of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia. And as the witness spoke about them, you can take them over, and I should like to have them exhibited as a unified exhibit. There are 27 decisions although there are, of course, more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will exhibit them for identification. They will be admitted for identification until they're translated and shown to be what they claim to be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 138 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, because my time is short. Let's look at some important issues. Is it true that at the beginning of the October 1990, activities began to intensify illegal arming of Croatia in collaboration with Slovenia? I'm sure you'll remember that during that period of time, the JNA uncovered nine illegal channels for smuggling weapons, et cetera. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Not that I know of. And that the JNA uncovered any such illegal channels, but I do know that the army disarmed the Slovene Territorial Defence in May that year, and this was already referred to. This is when the democratically elected authorities were put in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not taking this as cause and effect of any kind. I have here, for example, a certificate. It says the Republic of Slovenia, the Ministry of the Interior, confirming that a transport of weapons and ammunition passing through the Republic of Serbia is exclusively intended for the Defence Ministry of Croatia and contains the following, and then we have an enumeration of what it contains: 10.000 mines, 9.757.000 bullets, and so on and so forth. The Minister -- let me just read his name, what his name was. Jarnjak, and the stamp -- actually, his name is under the stamp so it's not very legible. Anyway, it's addressed to the Republic of Slovenia and the Ministry of the Interior. Is it true and correct that you participated in the arming of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want the witness to comment on the document, he must see it. Let the witness see the document and comment on it. Mr. Kucan, would you look at that document, please, and if you can, identify it, confirm it is what the accused said it is, perhaps you could give us a date for it, and then went on it as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 7th of December, 1992. But of course, it is the first time I see this document, however, I do not see really anything questionable here on this document because the accused in his previous questions said that there were illegal channels for acquiring weapons for -- well, I do not know about illegal channels. There was a legal channel, and for this procurement it is the authorities of republics that had the responsibility, and otherwise, there was really no need for republics to purchase arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at that time too there was an embargo imposed by the international community on any kind of import of arms into Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: This was before the international recognition of Slovenia and Croatia, as we can conclude from the date indicated, and therefore, this embargo did not concern us. This was after the withdrawal of the JNA from -- excuse me, that was at the time of recognition, recognition of both states which then individually, as individual states, took measures to be able to safeguard and protect their sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the embargo apply to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The embargo concerned the sales of arms and was valid for the sales of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to hear this. My question was whether the embargo applied to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and your answer was that the embargo was only on the sale of weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a document of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, signed by Azim Karamehmedovic, a certificate by authority of the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, I declare that I, born on such-and-such a date, member of the Crisis Staff, et cetera, that equipment amounting to the 1.850.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This sounds very much like a statement by somebody. What you could put to the witness, if you wish, if he can deal with it, if it's anything to do with him, you can put what it has in it, but you can't exhibit a statement by somebody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a statement. It is a certificate by authority of the president of the republic, Alija Izetbegovic, and it says: "1.850.000 German marks, equipment obtained from the Republic of Slovenia, that it will be paid for within the shortest delay, and until the date of payment we provide as guarantees to the Republic of Slovenia our helicopter which is on the territory of Slovenia. If the BH fails to pay this amount, this helicopter will remain permanently in the possession of Slovenia." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date? What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 29th of May, 1992, which means during the period when the embargo was in force. And as the witness himself said, related to the sale of weapons, and this document talks about the sale of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To save time. Yes, I will. I'll show it to him, Mr. May, and I would like to tender it into evidence. But before I show it to him, I have something else I wish to show him. A specification of needs for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is addressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. We cannot deal with a whole plethora of documents. Show the witness the certificate and let the witness comment on it. Do one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But my time is short, otherwise, I'd be glad to do that. Attached to the certificate is this document from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Slovenia, addressed to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, indicating which weapons were involved. Here you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, could you look, please, at this document and confirm, please, if it is what the accused says it is, and if you have any comments to make about them, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all about embargo. It is not forbidden that states purchase weapons for their defence. And the question this document concerns was carried out by our Minister of Defence and the responsible body of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There are documents to this effect in the archives of the Republic of Slovenia, in the Ministry of Defence, and should the Prosecution wish so, they can obtain this exhibit in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the specification signed by Alija Izetbegovic, how many million rounds, how many rifles, et cetera? Written by hand and signed by Alija Izetbegovic. You're familiar with his signature, just as I am.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: As far as thousands of rifles are concerned, 1.000 rifles and not several thousand rifles. And as mentioned before, there were competent bodies in Slovenia dealing with this, and it is these bodies that can provide accurate answers. The fact is, however, that in January 1993, a decision was adopted to the effect of which Slovenia is no longer to take part in aid or help, be it with weapons or, for instance, in terms of transport across its territory, either to Croatia or to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will have these documents exhibited, marked for identification. The relevance of them we will deal with in due course. The Croatian one first, please, and then the BiH one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the certificate dated the 7th of December, 1992, is Defence Exhibit 139, marked for identification. And the certificate signed by Alija Izetbegovic is Defence Exhibit 140, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you did participate in arming Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right? That is not at issue, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to accept such an assertion, because first of all, we should establish where the weapons that the Yugoslav army took with it upon withdrawal was headed for, and then also once it established that they no longer needed weapons for the military service for reserve forces, and then only can we see whether Bosnia and Herzegovina was capable of organising its own defence or not under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether it is challenged that you participated in arming Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: And my answer is: Why was it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's a very good answer. Is it true, please, that the president of your commission for establishing Slovenia's involvement in arming Bosnia and Herzegovina, called Rudolf Odbor, requested that the commission be disbanded? You had a commission to establish the involvement of Slovenia in the arming of Bosnia and Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I do not know this name. Can you repeat this person's name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have it noted here. Rudolf Mofe, according to my notes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, probably a deputy of the Slovene -- Slovene Assembly Rudolf Moge, who headed this committee. It was one of the committees that was there to establish the facts in connection with the weapons in Slovenia beginning with the disarmament of the Territorial Defence forces. And these reports can be found in the archives and records in Slovenia, and actually, this is something that is not yet concluded in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been completed yet. So let us move on, please. In paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that the Serbs looked upon Yugoslavia as a country enabling all Serbs to live in one state, which is a fact; all the Serbs lived in Yugoslavia. But then you go on to say that non-Serb nations saw Yugoslavia as protecting groups, which I -- as I find this quite unbelievable, I'm asking you now, surely you know that the constitution of Yugoslavia guaranteed to all citizens, regardless of their nationality or faith, equal civil rights, judicial and every other protection up to the level of the federal state. The constitution didn't protect any groups but the citizens who, therefore, logically believed that they were living in one state. It applied to everyone, without any discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Such a statement certainly is unbelievable, but I didn't make such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said it was unbelievable, and it is paragraph 7 of your statement. But if you say it's unbelievable, then I won't read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I say it is. I assert it's unbelievable, by I also insist I didn't state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here it says, "Non-Serb nations saw Yugoslavia as protecting the groups while as the Serbs viewed it as a country that allowed all Serbs to live in the same state." I read this from your statement, but I'm glad that you also consider it to be unbelievable. Let us move on then. You claim that the JNA did not recognise the collective Supreme Command after Tito. Did you assert that or is this again an unbelievable fabrication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, concerning the previous assertion, I'm sure it must have been an erroneous interpretation. Yugoslavia didn't protect groups, and the Slovenian nation is not a group. I spoke about that. As far as the JNA is concerned, it is true it did not recognise the Supreme Command. And in the sessions held in March 1991, after -- concerning which a lot has been written about, it was -- became clear that the JNA, its leadership, wanted to place itself above the Supreme Commander, i.e., the Presidency of the SFRY. And let me make it clear already at the 13th Congress of the League of Communists in 1986, there was quite a heated debate which was stated there, and the -- concerning the fact that if the League of Communists is not capable of resolving the situation, then the JNA will step in and attempt to resolve it. Transcripts of that exist, and you can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. This is in paragraph 27 -- 26, rather, that it didn't recognise the Presidency. The example you use is incorrect. You say the army did not want a state of emergency. On the contrary, it proposed such a state of emergency but the Presidency did not accept that proposal. It did not adopt it. There was such a proposal. So your example is incorrect too.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be needed to have a close look of what had -- what's happening there and the time. The books of Borisav Jovic and Vjelko Kadijevic speak clear what was the nature of the JNA leadership and how it responded to the dilemmas faced by Yugoslavia. In order to have a better understanding of this, let me mention a detail. One of the greatest opponents at the 14th Congress of the League of Communists was the proposal to have a civilian control over the JNA and also to accept the civilian serving of the military service as well as also not serving due to reasons of conscience, as conscientious objectors.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of today's testimony, Mr. Nice produced a transcript of one of my speeches from a Central Committee meeting at which there was quite a bit of manipulation, as I can see, with words. Institutional, and non-institutional, but in the interest of Yugoslavia, and so on. Do you recollect that this institutional and non-institutional related to rallies that were being held at which the citizens expressed their political dissatisfaction or their political options, which were widely reported on, saying not a single flower had been stamped upon, not a single windowpane broken, but on the contrary, people were carrying flowers and singing. And in the leadership of Yugoslavia at the time spoke about such rallies as being non-institutional and said that problems could not be resolved non-institutionally. Therefore, this term related to those mass rallies, and what you did is to equate non-institutional with non-constitutional. Why would public rallies be non-constitutional or illegal if freedom of assembly was guaranteed by the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, this interpretation is not correct. At that meeting, we discussed changes, and it was said that if changes do not occur institutionally, they will occur uninstitutionally, and it won't be according to the procedures, but it will be introduced by the will of the people, will of the nation, be it by the people of the nation or of the street. We asserted that on the street it is possible to express the dissatisfaction but that the street cannot bring changes and that it cannot formulate a positive programme. These rallies were not such an innocent matter. There was, for example, the Vojvodina leadership which did not accept the decisions of the Belgrade government.
