And after two rallies, they were replaced. Later, it was the turn of Montenegro. So it's not a question of a right to assembly and rally and expressing of dissatisfaction, and it all ended with a ban on that rally which was planned for the 1st of December, 1989, in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the citizens of Montenegro rally? Oh, I see. It ended with the prohibition of the rally planned for Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Who planned it? Slovenes did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that too. Now, in this speech of mine that was quoted from by Mr. Nice, I say that jeopardy for the system reached its climax in Kosovo in the physical, political, and cultural violence against Serbs and Montenegrins. Are you denying that in those days there was a lot of violence against Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I know that there was violence, also mutual violence. I also Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. presented to the Court my position. I said that the Serb national issue is very complex, that the complexity is reflected also through the tense relations, particularly in Kosovo. And in 1985, I was at the head of a group which was to study the constitutional relationship in the Socialist Republic of Serbia, the two autonomous provinces and the republic within the federal structure, in order to introduce some improvement for the improvement of the entire situation in the Republic of Serbia and within the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I say here, since I was quoted out of context, that the threats reached a climax in violence. And then the next sentence: "In environments or in connection with problems that were not heeded and which could not be addressed by institutional means, as a result, there were large-scale and public protests by the citizens at public rallies." Therefore, I am saying that the institutions did not react, the citizens protest at rallies and bring pressure to bear on institutions. And then I go on to say that is how it always was in human society. But true, with the development of society and its greater organisation and greater democratisation, man's ability to effect changes in society by institutional means increase and that the requests for a pro-Yugoslav orientation are directed to activate the system of elected institutions. That is what I spoke about. And I defend the right of citizens to express their views at rallies which, as I hope you too will admit, were not violent. Is that right or not, Mr. Kucan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I don't know what you're really asking me on the basis of this very long explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking whether those rallies why were violent in any sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: This would be best answered by those who had to resign but were -- although elected to their posts, and resigned on the basis of these rallies. As I remember from 1981 onwards, in Kosovo three times state of emergency was introduced. But let me say, state of emergency and violence couldn't stop violence in general. It just bred additional violence and new political solutions had to be found and by strengthening institutions and not by making, creating difficulties in the work of these institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic. Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I simply cannot cross-examine the witness fully in five minutes. Mr. Nice spent at least ten minutes on this one speech of mine, and I have to ask the witness certain things about Kosovo as well, which are very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must move on to that then. You were given two hours, and in five minutes -- five minutes the two hours -- don't interrupt. Five minutes' time, the two hours will be up. So move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm asking you to give me a little more time, because my time is expiring in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could I raise a matter, and that is that this witness be recalled to continue his evidence on another occasion? It's often used that important people are too busy to give up their time when the experience might be that important people are more able to create space in their diaries to give up time, and it's harder for those less elevated to provide time to come to these institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can have a quarter of an hour more. Mr. Kay, we hear what you say, and no doubt the Prosecution has heard it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I was saying, as they're selectively quoting things out of context, that is Mr. Nice quoting certain things from my speech, and the witness also speaks about Serbia's pro-centralist position and Slovenia's more liberal attitude, I say, for instance, in that very speech for which I'm grateful to the opposite for making it available to me as I have great difficulty getting hold of documents, I say that an important fact is being neglected and that is we are a federation. Yugoslavia is a federal community, all nations and nationalities living in it, which means they are all equal amongst themselves or, rather, that they have an equal position in the economic, political, and cultural life of the country in which they live. This undisputed assertion must, for all these reasons, be made clear that a collection of votes can resolve the situation whereas inequality can upset the federation. So I am speaking in favour of the equality of nations and republics, and that is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us save time by saying that we have this speech, and we have that passage or the passage you referred to about Yugoslavia being a federal community. Yes. Anything else you want to refer to and any question you want to ask the witness, do it quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have questions, and I'm going to have to ask them quickly. That seems to be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But have I understood you correctly and it is not a typing error once again; you were aware of the fact that in Kosovo the strike, the famous strike, hunger strike by the miners on the old square was rigged and in fact that the miners did receive food? Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that, and I think it's irrelevant. It's irrelevant whether they received the food or not. It's a fact that they were on strike, that they were in the pit against -- in full or greater awareness concerning the changing of the status of the Kosovo province.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that Kosovo and Vojvodina, that their autonomy was rescinded. Is that what you state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I think I was quite precise when there was the officially -- the autonomy was officially rescinded. As I understood it, the then-policy of Serbia and the position of the Serbian leadership, it was essential to preserve the three votes together -- the three votes, the two votes coming from the two provinces. And therefore, the changes in the Serbian constitution significantly reduced the autonomy of the two provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that it says in the constitution that two autonomous provinces exist, those of Kosovo and Vojvodina and that they enjoy autonomy, that that is what it says in the constitution or, rather, the constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Well, that was written, also put down in the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it also says so in the constitution of Serbia, doesn't it? So neither -- the constitution of Serbia did not abolish the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija and Vojvodina. And second, is it also true there was an error made here when you had said that the members of the SFRY Presidency from the provinces were replaced? You know that the Presidency member by the name of Zelenovic was elected as Prime Minister of the government of Serbia and before that he was a member of the Yugoslavia state Presidency for Vojvodina province, and as he took up his new duties, the Assembly of Vojvodina elected a new Presidency member. Isn't that how it was? Serbia did not replace him. On the contrary, he was the Prime Minister designate asked to set up a government and there was a seat left empty for the Vojvodina Presidency because he couldn't keep two posts. So the Vojvodina Assembly elected a new member to the Yugoslav state Presidency. Wasn't that how it was, Mr. Kucan, or is what you say correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Formally it is so, but de facto, the events evolved under pressure of those rallies which we've already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, well, you don't really assume that somebody was designated Prime Minister of Serbia formally, officially, elected in the Assembly in order to de facto be replaced in his post as Yugoslav Presidency member? I'm sure you're not going to say anything nonsensical as that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I am not saying that this is nonsensical or that it happened due to the nonsense, but I'm just saying these replacements occurred due to certain facts, and if it's relevant, then we have to go back into those documents which exist of the time and which are in the files. But I'm not an historian which would follow these events, and I don't think that this court is writing a history -- the history either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. This court is endeavouring to recut history, to tailor history, in fact. As you denied what I claimed a moment ago, I'm going to read out your own paragraph, and it is paragraph 57, where you say the following: "Linked to paragraph as to how Milosevic used the army, deployed the army," and it says in brackets, "Kucan's comments on the Death of Yugoslavia, linked to the events in the mines at the Stari Trg old square, this took place at the regular Presidency meeting. We did not receive information of this kind. The protest was organised by the Slovenian opposition and the party. I was supposed to speak there. It was going to be a staged strike, in fact, that the miners were not on a hunger strike, that they were getting food into the mine, since it was uncertain how long the session would last," and so on and so forth. Now, what does all this mean? I have several questions, specific ones. First: This took place during the period of time when I myself was the party president and not the President of Serbia, this strike in the old square. And we were there at the Presidency meeting together on Stari Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Trg, the party Presidency. So what use of the army could there have been on our side or on the part of any republic, because Janez Drnovsek was president of the Yugoslav state Presidency during that period of time. So was the decisions which you mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must have a question in this. I'm just trying to understand what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking something with respect to paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could I have used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just ask a specific question and the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I use the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Is that the question? The army could be used on the basis of the decision of the Presidency, and that is what I insisted upon also when the army was used in Slovenia. The Presidency didn't issue such an order then, but it did decide on the use of the army in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Presidency of Yugoslavia, wasn't it, made the decision with respect to any army activities in Kosovo. The Yugoslav state Presidency made decisions of that kind, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. The Presidency of Yugoslavia, which had always decided on the basis of a proposal. And I don't know who submitted such a proposal on the basis of which then they decided on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know either, to tell you the truth. But the Presidency of Yugoslavia made the decision, so I assume that it's common knowledge to both of us, you and I, that none of the presidents of the republics could have wielded an influence on the army and we could have just been received by the top military echelons, we were not able to give them orders of any kind. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I never asserted anything else. I don't know from where this idea that I asserted that you were the ones who were issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I wanted to hear, because, Mr. Kucan, it was precisely because of the manipulations of the opposite side over there that here in this summary for which they say you did not authorise it, that they are their notes and so on, says regarding the paragraph on Milosevic using the army with respect to the events that took place at Stari Trg, and so on. I couldn't believe that you yourself said something like that. So I would like to have this manipulation eliminated, and I'm happy to see that you have confirmed this in this way. Now, let me ask you something with respect to Kosovo, one more thing relating to Kosovo. Is it true that you supported the separatists, separatism and terrorism in Kosovo which -- and the separatists being intensively armed via Slovenia and in the centres of Territorial Defence of Slovenia they were being trained, that is to say the members of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. One thing at a time. Let me say this, that we have received information that we can in fact have this courtroom for an extra half hour to try and accommodate all those who want to ask questions. So we will break in a few minutes for ten minutes and then we will consider how long anybody else should have. Now, Mr. Kucan, it's put that you were supporting two things in Kosovo. It's put first of all you were supporting separatism, and then it's suggested you were also supporting terrorism - and I should say three things - and then that the separatists in Kosovo were being armed via Slovenia and being trained by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, most energetically I refute these allegations. Let me say that nobody from the leadership, Slovenian leadership supported their separatism. We never trained on our territory. We always insisted on a political solution of the Kosovo problem, and when there was a widespread outbreak of violence in Kosovo with the exodus of Albanians, and when the violence turned the other way, and let me say that will not prevent one violence with other sources of violence. And I can accept no accusations of this type for myself or anybody in the leadership of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will break now for ten minutes, for the interpreters. We will come back and decide how long anybody should have from now on. Any re-examination I anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few questions but I can deal with them in a compact way, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have another ten minutes, if you want, to ask the witness any questions. Mr. Tapuskovic, 20 minutes thereafter. And, Mr. Nice, you've got five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Strove for separatism in Kosovo, I have Agim Zogaj book here, "A Dialogue with Naim Maljoku," and he says to him -- first of all he tells him about the meeting in Cankarjev Dom which was held and it was support to them. Then he goes on to speak about close cooperation with Janez Jansa, and then we have information about the training of their members who later took part in the KLA. And I'm going to read out on page 43, this is what he says with respect to the rally that you forbid, and the Serbs came from Kosovo expecting to find solidarity on the part of the Slovenian people for the sufferings they experienced over there, he says: "I and Fadilj Demiri one evening were watching the news bulletin, and when the bulletin began with 500.000 armed Serbs coming to Ljubljana --" that's how the news bulletin started. So you -- this initiative of the Serbs from Kosovo who were the victims of Albanian terrorism, when they turned up, you -- to tell the citizens of Slovenia, as they had done in other localities, there was no violence anywhere, you forbid them to come and to state the truth about their sufferings and even on your television news bulletin you say that 500.000 armed Serbs are on their way to Ljubljana. Now, during those years and when the meeting took place, was there any arming at all and shooting at those rallies or was there testimony about the truly difficult situation that the Serbs were facing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: So there is a number of questions raised by the accused and also assessment. First of all, I don't know -- I know neither the book nor the authors of the book quoted by the accused. I refute, and I will refute also in the future that we supported any type of Albanian separatism in Kosovo. The accused knows full well my position -- what my position is, that Kosovo is a part of the territory of Serbia and that it was a part, as such, of SFRY, and that is why also at the meeting in Ljubljana, which was a meeting of support to the miners in Stari Trg in Kosovo, there there was -- no word was said that we support any separatism, secession. We opted for a political solution because it's not possible to achieve any other type of solution for this problem. Why did we ban that rally of truth? Because the bodies of internal order evaluated that there would be -- conflicts would break out and unrest. And Slovenes didn't want people who -- Slovenes didn't want people attending rallies to come to tell them the truth about Kosovo. They believed their other channels for that. And we didn't have propaganda which would speak unilaterally of the situation in Kosovo. We knew it enough to know that it was a complex solution and that a solution cannot be imposed, neither to Serbs, Montenegrins or Albanians, that they must find a modus vivendi for this life together and also a rationale for that. We never considered that it would be irrational to keep Kosovo in Yugoslavia, but the Serbs sometimes asserted that that was our line. And Borisav Jovic wrote something along these lines in his book, and I will -- I don't know whether it is authentic or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I hope that you will remember the demonstrations held in 1980, as far as back as that, organised by the separatists where the main slogan was "Kosovo Republic" and that the main goal was the independence of Kosovo and conjunction with Albania. There was no Milosevic on the political scene of the day. There was nothing about what we're talking and testifying about here in quite a distorted fashion. But do you remember that? Do you consider that this support lent to this kind of policy served the purpose of stability for Serbian Yugoslavia or served the purpose of destabilising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is that the witness is talking about this support lent to the miners, the alleged hunger strike which was staged, rigged, without entering into what was called for. And what was called for was that the goals be fulfilled, which were voiced in 1980 and proclaimed, and that was Kosovo Republic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that so, Mr. Kucan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that there was no support for Kosovo separatism. He didn't support that. The Slovenes didn't. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he personally did not support it, but I think that Janez Jansa, for example, and the whole camaderia around him did indeed support this. And you can find that in this book here, and I would like to have the book exhibited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know quite well we don't exhibit books unless there is some extract that the witness can personally vouch for, which we did this morning, and that was the only exception. But you're putting that Janez Jansa and what you describe as the camaderia around him did support it. Mr. Kucan, can you help us with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Janez Jansa was the minister in the first government after the first free democratic elections. I cooperated with him throughout his occupying this post of minister. And never in my formal and informal contacts with him could I have an indication that anybody was supporting separatism of Albanians in Kosovo or Kosovo Republic, and I will not reiterate what I already stated. We could do only that if we hated Serbs. But I insist: We were not in conflict with the Serbian nation. We always understood how difficult it was to resolve the Serb national issue. And certainly in the Balkans, it's one of the most difficult. Where we differed was how this problem could be solved and that it wouldn't be at the expense of other nations and nationalities. And that is why recriminations concerning the support of Slovenes for Albanian separatism is not founded, and you will not find it in no documents of the government or other bodies of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would need at least two questions, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. please, Mr. May. One -- this one now and one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, I'm sure you will remember that in Ljubljana in November 1985, a discussion was held between Slovenian and Serbian intellectuals to discuss the situation in the then-Yugoslavia. It was a group around the Nova Revija, journal, with some theoreticians, Paca [phoen], Ljubancic [phoen], Hribar, Apic, Hermaun [phoen], and others, and it was incontestable at the time that Slovenian nationalism and the anti-Yugoslav sentiments had been undisguised at a time when Milosevic wasn't on the political arena, when there was no Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences in the sense that you mention later on. Is that right or not? We're talking about 1985, and I'm sure you know full well what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: This meeting did take place, a meeting between some Serbian and Slovenian intellectuals. That is a fact that is universally known. However, I have no knowledge whether at that time Slovene nationalism broke out or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One last but quick question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Point 11, paragraph 11 of your statement, you say the Kingdom of Yugoslavia lived with very different internal differences. I don't think that sentence has been translated very well, but anyway, I'm interested in the second sentence: "The occupation in 1941, shortened the agony; Slovenia capitulated basically because it did not see itself fighting to save a country that was not really their own." Did you really say that, that Slovenia capitulated because it saw no reason to preserve a country which was not its own? Please. And within this context, the context of this question, tell me, where was your family during World War II and how come you have the name -- your first name is Milan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You need not answer either of those last questions. The question about what happened in 1941, if you want to answer it, Mr. Kucan, you can. If you don't, there's no need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer this question, because there has been a lot of speculation in the Serbian press about it, and there seems to be continuing. My family lived in Prekmurje in Krizurci [phoen], which is a part of Slovenia close to the Hungarian border. This was the part of Slovenia that was occupied by the Hungarians. My mother, who was a teacher, was arrested and was imprisoned for shorter periods of time. My father, who returned after the capitulation of the Yugoslav Royal Army, was drafted by the Germans, sent to the Russian front. He there decided, with some other combatants, to join voluntarily the POWs and when in the Soviet Union the Yugoslav brigade was established, he joined it, and together with the brigade he returned to Yugoslavia and he was killed in the battle for Cacak, a city in Serbia. He was in fact wounded there, and then he was taken to a hospital but he died because of bleeding, and he was buried there, and in 1954, when we brought his remains to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I really don't know how I will be able to do my job today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please, Mr. Kucan, tell me first whether Kristan Milan -- Ivan is one of the constitutional judges in the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia who passed rulings in connection with these decision and these amendments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Ivan Kristan was one of the two constitutional judges from Slovenia serving on the court at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to draw the attention of the Court right now that an expert witness in this case in connection with constitutional matters is a Slovene who was a judge in the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, and this is something that we shall have to bear in mind. So Ivan Kristan is an expert witness in this case and he was a judge in the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So my first question now is, Mr. Kucan, did you ever hear of the existence, before 1991, or before August 1991, to be more precise, any kind of criminal plan in connection with the commission of crimes ethnic cleansing, or genocide?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Where should such a plan have been drawn up and existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Such a plan, according to the indictment, should have existed in the first place in Serbia, that there should have -- that there was allegedly a plan to commit the crime of ethnic cleansing and eventually the crime of genocide. Did you hear from anyone that any such thing had been prepared in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No, I never heard of it, and I never said anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now as you have the book -- this book in front of you, the book by General Kadijevic, will you please look at a chapter headed by the more important events in the final stages of the break-up of Yugoslavia and the attacks on the JNA in Slovenia. This is page 99 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please find the chapter, the important events from the final stages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't have the book. It was merely an extract which was admitted and was put in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you something? A moment ago, you said that in Slovenia it was not accepted for commands in the army to be spoken in Serbian. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't the dominant language in Yugoslavia Serbo-Croatian, and throughout the history after the Second World War, we never spoke of Serbian or Croatian but only about the Serbo-Croatian language, and orders were expressed in the Serbo-Croatian language. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Now, you see, you are talking about a dominant language. I have no knowledge of a dominant language. All languages of nations were equal in the territories in which they lived, including the languages of the ethnicities. We never said anything to that effect, that we're against the language of commands, although we had certain reservations. What I said is the following: The official language in the JNA was the language of all nations and ethnicities and that the Slovene language had not been used on the Slovene territory in the armed forces at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it was necessary to have commands in the JNA in a language that would be understandable for all the nations and nationalities. I think that the Slovenes understood both Serbian and Croatian very well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: They understood it relatively well. However, the opposite never was the case. The Serbs, the Croats, and the Macedonians never made the effort to understand the Slovene language. But this seems to be quite irrelevant to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasted time on this that I shouldn't have. Is it true that in Kadijevic's book it says that, by significance and time, there was the attack on the JNA in Yugoslavia stemmed from the 1974 constitution. Then and later, acts were taken through the JNA against the Yugoslav state. What would be your comments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: This is a very severe political condemnation for which I see absolutely no political argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in October 1984, there was a meeting of the then-leaders of Slovenia and a decision taken to engage in an open political conflict and attack against the JNA through the youth and to declare the JNA already then as an occupying army? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: No. This is an army construct that I'm quite familiar with. I met it occasionally. And it's quite interesting that -- Your Honours, this is a sort of construct that I was faced with during the party sessions. Let me emphasise that the League of Communists of Yugoslavia comprised the parties that had existed in the individual republics and Autonomous Provinces. However, the army had its own party organisation as well. And this organisation had the same weight and the same rights as were the rights and weight of the republic's communist party organisations. This is what I'm emphasising to show to you that the army had a very strong ideological and political stamp and that its ideological homeland was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that those attacks were particularly fierce between 1984 and 1988 prior to the adoption of the constitutional amendments in 1988 when JNA soldiers who came from all over Yugoslavia were humiliated, spat upon, and even beaten in some cases? Is that true or not? This is something that Mr. Kadijevic speaks about in his book.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: You are using "attacked by." This is the terminology of the JNA and the political leaders in the JNA. The question was the following: Can the army, the privileges of the army, the procedures and actions, the plans of the army, large projects such as the manufacturing of a Yugoslav tank, a Yugoslav supersonic aircraft, can this sort of issues and questions be described and written about in the press? Since the tank project did go through, the aircraft project did not, it had been obvious that the JNA was launching these projects not only to cover its own capability requirements but also to export them. An article entitled "Mamula Go Home" - Mamula was the then Minister of Defence - and this article described the selling of weapons to Ethiopia, a very poor country at that time. These articles and others were qualified as attacks on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... relevant.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: It is relevant because you are talking about the attacks on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of August, 1988, was there a meeting of the Presidency of the SFRY at which these problems were discussed? And the representative of Slovenia rejected all the proposals made to prevent such things occurring again. Do you know anything about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I apologise. I -- because the speaker is speaking very fast, I couldn't get either the date or the event in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I could speak very slowly, but really, under these circumstances, I wonder whether I'm able to perform my duties at all. I really find myself in a very difficult situation because there are many things that I would like to draw your attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure there are. If you want to put them into writing, you can, and we'll deal with them. But you know, this witness has been cross-examined for two and a half hours already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to appeal to you. I've already discussed this with Mr. Kay and will make something in writing, but under these circumstances, it is absolutely impossible for me Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to cross-examine in 20 minutes, and there are many issues which I really think would be interesting for you. It is only now that I come to my main point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put your main point now. If you want to put them to the witness, do. Otherwise, we'll just go on to the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So I must come to the most important thing which is also contained in Mr. Kadijevic's book. With the collapse of the USSR, the possibility of military intervention from the West became quite clear and obvious. Is that clear, Mr. Kucan? Is that true, Mr. Kucan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I do not really know what sort of military interventions you're referring to and what you have in mind by putting this question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't speak of any military intervention. I referred to the collapse of the Soviet Union, the toppling of the Berlin Wall, and all the other events that occurred at that time. And according to the notes that were made on the 5th/6th of November, 2002, you said that Slovenia's path towards independence could not have taken place without the collapse of the Soviet Union and the reunification of Germany; is that correct? That you realised what the problems would be even before Gorbachev, and that you spoke to Gorbachev about this. This is contained in the notes of your interview.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: My testimonies, if they're authentic, you can read the following: I understand that the Yugoslav crisis was a part of the wider crisis of the socialist world that had compromised itself and that it culminated through the toppling of the Berlin Wall and through the disintegration of the Soviet Union. This is true and this is also what the facts of history have confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true what General Kadijevic says in his book, that there were certain influences from abroad and that to justify the aggression there were two variants; the first, if the defenders of the unity of Yugoslavia resort to force first, they have justification because, in quotation marks, unitary Greater Serbian forces are trying to topple democratically regimes all over Yugoslavia. And the second variant, if that does not happen, then Slovenia and Croatia would be forced to use force to impose their will, and through the media war the world would be convinced that they are the victims of gross aggression. And what happened was this second option, second variant. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we're very assisted. These are the opinions of General Kadijevic. Now, I'm not sure that it's of great assistance putting them to the witness. We've heard his evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge May, was there any external influence over Slovenia so that it should attack the JNA first to provoke what happened in Yugoslavia? Was there any such influence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll let the witness answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With his ideas, concerns, and fears that he harboured, I had never been informed by Mr. Kadijevic. Now, I emphasised it before that no external influences, no external interests, and no external incentives that would run our activities had existed. We never followed anybody's instructions, we're not doing it at this point in time. We are trying to live within a democratic community of nations, and we are trying to do it to the best of our abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You stated here that all you wanted was independence and to prevent violence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I said that we wanted to achieve independence and that we wanted to achieve it on the basis of an agreement without the use of force. We wanted, on the basis of a consensus, to regulate our past and to discuss how we can continue to live together with those who had, until then, lived on the territory of the SFRY. This is what is also written down in all of the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen, and it was shown in Slovenia quite recently, a film by an Austrian TV station at the Holmec frontier crossing, a group of JNA soldiers were shown with their hands raised in a token of surrender, coming out of a trench, on whom Slovenian TO members opened fire, upon which they all fell back into the trenches. Have you seen that film and did this take place or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: A TV coverage of an event already mentioned here before. I emphasised before that a special committee was established in Slovenia to investigate this event. It did not establish that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need to trouble you to go over that again. This is the Holmec incident which has been referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm repeating this only because on this clip it is visible to see the men with their hands raised, upon which they were shot at. That's why I'm repeating. They were surrendering whereas they were shot at. Fire was opened at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've already dealt with this. He said there was an investigation. Now, we must ask you to come to an end, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it really is difficult. I'll put my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I received from the Prosecution an interview of Kucan on the 21st of December, 1993 to the Mladina newspaper in Slovenia. When the war broke out in Croatia, the position of the Defence Ministry was adopted, and that is to help Croatia with weapons and that that would be the best defence for Slovenia. Is that right or not? This is what you stated on 21st of December, 1993, and this was published in the Mladina newspaper -- magazine. If you were against violence, why did you assist Croatia with weapons and, after that, Bosnia as well? Though according to your original assessments, you considered that to have been a civil war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: I do not know what is the question. Are you asking me about the civil war or about something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and deal with it this way: What is alleged is that in an interview in a newspaper in 1993, you said the position was to help Croatia with weapons when the war broke out there, and that would be the defence for Slovenia. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that in this particular interview, and I am convinced that this was a justified act. At that time, there was only a cease-fire in Slovenia. The war went on to Croatia, and since Croatia was attacked, helping Croatia, we indeed believed that that would be a defence for Slovenia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So Croatia was attacked or were all the barracks in Croatia surrounded and the soldiers left without bread, water, electricity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, that's something about which we've heard a lot of evidence. We will have to decide about it. I don't think we need trouble the witness with it. Do you want us to have the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has it. I can give you the number. It is R0336514, disclosed on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nice. I'm afraid two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan, single word answers, if you please, without being offensive, just to save time. We've heard of customs money. At the declaration of independence, did Slovenia have entitlement to monies at the central bank? If so, did it get them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The customs monies is a special example. It was collected by Slovenia, placed on a special account, and this account would be also decided upon on the basis of the final solution for the former Yugoslavia. However, the Republic of Serbia intervened, intervened in the monetary system January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You still have substantial claims outstanding as a result? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: Where the foreign currency reserves have been placed, we don't know the amounts and that is why we're asking also for the financial statements of the National Bank of Yugoslavia, because this could be an item in the secession negotiations which have not been completed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mass demonstrations spoken of by the accused, for example in Vojvodina, arising spontaneously or, as you understand it, stimulated from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: As far as the conditions of life of Serbs and Montenegrins living in Kosovo, there was a lot of anguish, a lot of difficulties between Serbs, Montenegrins, and Albanians. And if mass demonstrations -- a rally didn't take place in 1987 where the accused stated nobody has a right to beat you, this referred to Serbs and Montenegrins, one would think that these meetings were really spontaneous. But in fact, if he said nobody has a right to beat anybody in Kosovo, I would have -- hold my beliefs even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The weapons paid for by Slovenia held at its Territorial Defence bases, did it retain those weapons or did it lose them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUCAN
utterances.text: The weapons which were taken away, the JNA then, when withdrawing, it took with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am not going to stretch my time limit. Your Honour, I would ask, there was one exercise we could have done with the Jovic diary on the allegations of the Slovenia starting the war. I'd ask you to consider the Jovic extracts, to which I'm adding one, for the relevant period to see how consistent they are with that as an allegation. Providing you've got the documents, there's nothing more I need deal with. Then there's the constitutional decisions that were placed in evidence. There is another one that we have which relates to or comes from February 1990, but we can deal with those through the expert witness Dr. Kristan when he comes, and I hope I haven't gone beyond my two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kucan, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It is concluded and you are free to go. We will adjourn. 9:00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a short administrative matter, if it's possible to deal with now about the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The problem is that we must be out of here because there is another hearing due. We'll deal with it in writing, if we can. If you put something in writing, we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.04 p.m.,
